# Overview



This page introduces **bAIes-IDP-OpenMM** at a conceptual level: what the project is, the scientific problem it solves, how its workflow fits together, and the technology stack a beginner needs to have in place. No prior experience with molecular dynamics or AI structure prediction is assumed. By the end of this page you will understand the project's purpose and know exactly where to go next in the documentation.

## What Is bAIes-IDP-OpenMM?

bAIes-IDP-OpenMM is the **OpenMM implementation of bAIes**, a method that produces *atomic resolution ensemble predictions of intrinsically disordered proteins using AI structure predictors*. Rather than predicting a single rigid 3D structure, bAIes combines the statistical power of AlphaFold-family predictors with physics-based molecular dynamics sampling to generate a **distribution of conformations** that describes how these flexible proteins actually behave in solution. The method is peer-reviewed: it was published in *Nature Communications* with an accompanying preprint, both of which the README asks users to cite.

![Visual Abstract](https://github.com/COSBlab/bAIes-IDP-OpenMM/blob/main/Visual_Abstract.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L3-L13)

## Why Ensembles Instead of a Single Structure?

Beginners arriving from classical structural biology are used to one protein → one structure. **Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) break that assumption**: they do not fold into a single stable shape, so any single prediction is fundamentally incomplete. bAIes therefore targets the correct object of study — the *conformational ensemble* — by propagating AI-derived restraints into an OpenMM simulation that samples many valid conformations. This reframing (from "a structure" to "an ensemble") is the single most important conceptual shift before reading further; the scientific details are developed step by step in the [Intrinsically Disordered Protein Ensembles](6-intrinsically-disordered-protein-ensembles) chapter.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7)

## The bAIes Workflow at a Glance

Before examining the diagram, note the prerequisite idea: bAIes is a **pipeline**, not a monolithic program. Each stage transforms an output of the previous stage, and each stage is covered in depth by its own chapter in this documentation. The following diagram shows the four conceptual stages end to end:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["AI structure predictors<br/>AlphaFold distograms<br/>+ MSA subsampling"] --> B["Statistical refinement<br/>ensemble-averaged restraints<br/>maximum entropy"]
    B --> C["OpenMM molecular dynamics<br/>force-field sampling<br/>GPU or CPU"]
    C --> D["Atomic-resolution IDP<br/>conformational ensemble"]
    D --> E["Trajectory analysis<br/>convergence and validation"]
```

Reading left to right: **AI structure predictors** supply distance information (distograms) and sequence-alignment statistics; **statistical refinement** converts those predictions into ensemble-averaged restraints under maximum-entropy principles; **OpenMM molecular dynamics** physically samples conformations consistent with those restraints using a standard force field; and **analysis** assesses convergence and validates against experiment. Each arrow corresponds to a documented workflow, so a beginner can study the pipeline incrementally rather than all at once.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7)

## Technology Stack and Requirements

The installation footprint is deliberately minimal: per the README, *"to run bAIes with OpenMM, you just need a python environment with OpenMM installed."* There are no bespoke compiled dependencies in this repository — the environment is a standard conda environment with pinned versions chosen for reproducibility:

| Component | Pinned Version | Role | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.13 | Runtime environment | Created via conda (`conda create -n baies python=3.13`) |
| OpenMM | 8.3 | Molecular dynamics engine | Installed from `conda-forge` |
| CUDA | 13 | GPU acceleration | Set to a version supported by **both** your GPU driver and OpenMM; omit entirely on machines without a GPU to get the CPU build |
| Installation check | — | `python -m openmm.testInstallation` | Confirms OpenMM sees your hardware before you run anything |

The pinning strategy (`openmm=8.3 cuda-version=13`) is the one configuration decision beginners most often get wrong.

> [!TIP]
> The `cuda-version` pin is a **dual constraint**, not a preference: it must be supported by both your NVIDIA driver (check with `nvidia-smi`) and your OpenMM release. If you omit the pin on a GPU-less machine, conda silently falls back to the CPU build — which is valid, but orders of magnitude slower for production ensembles.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L16-L41)

## Repository Structure

This repository has an intentionally small footprint — it serves as the project's public entry point, carrying the visual abstract, the canonical citation list, and the environment setup guide:

```
bAIes-IDP-OpenMM/
├── README.md              # Project identity, citation list, environment setup guide
└── Visual_Abstract.png    # One-figure summary of the bAIes ensemble workflow
```

Notably, the README's final section ("Run bAIes") contains a heading but no inline execution commands within this repository. That is a deliberate structural signal, not an omission to worry about.

> [!TIP]
> This repository is the **documentation and identity companion** — the runnable code and its operational instructions live in the companion repository. If you cannot find a script here, you are not lost; you are looking in the right repo for the wrong artifact. The [Companion Repository Resources](4-companion-repository-resources) page maps where everything executable lives.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L5), [README.md](README.md#L43-L44)

# Quick Start



This page walks you from an empty machine to a verified, simulation-ready **bAIes-IDP-OpenMM** environment in three steps. The repository is intentionally lightweight — it ships a single `README.md` containing the canonical setup instructions and one visual abstract — so this Quick Start translates that README into a beginner-friendly, verified walkthrough. By the end, you will have a working OpenMM installation that recognizes your hardware and will know exactly which documentation page to open next.

## What This Repository Gives You

Before installing anything, it helps to know the shape of what you are working with. The repository root contains exactly two artifacts: the `README.md` documentation file and `Visual_Abstract.png`, the project's visual summary. This minimal structure is deliberate — bAIes-IDP-OpenMM is the **OpenMM implementation** of the bAIes method for generating atomic-resolution ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins using AI structure predictors, and the actual simulation logic is consumed from its companion resources rather than duplicated here.

```
bAIes-IDP-OpenMM/
├── README.md            # Canonical installation instructions (44 lines)
└── Visual_Abstract.png  # Project visual abstract (1000px wide, centered)
```

![Visual Abstract](https://github.com/COSBlab/bAIes-IDP-OpenMM/blob/main/Visual_Abstract.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L7), [Visual_Abstract.png](Visual_Abstract.png)

## Quick Start Flow at a Glance

The entire setup path is a linear dependency chain: create an isolated Python environment, install the OpenMM engine (choosing a GPU or CPU build), verify that OpenMM can actually see your hardware, then proceed to running simulations. The Mermaid diagram below makes this decision structure explicit — note that there is only one true branching point (GPU vs. CPU) and one verification gate before you are ready to run.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Start: fresh machine"] --> B{"Is conda available?"}
    B -->|"No"| B1["Install Miniconda / Miniforge"]
    B -->|"Yes"| C
    B1 --> C["conda create -n baies python=3.13"]
    C --> D["conda activate baies"]
    D --> E{"GPU available?"}
    E -->|"Yes"| F["conda install -c conda-forge openmm=8.3 cuda-version=13"]
    E -->|"No"| G["conda install -c conda-forge openmm=8.3"]
    F --> H["python -m openmm.testInstallation"]
    G --> H
    H --> I{"Platforms recognized?"}
    I -->|"Yes"| J["Environment ready → run bAIes"]
    I -->|"No / missing CUDA"| K["Fix driver–CUDA version match"]
    K --> F
    J --> L["Next: Companion Repository Resources"]
```

Read this diagram top-down: every box on the main path is a command you will run in the sections below, and the only loops are failure-recovery paths. If you are on a CPU-only machine, you simply skip the GPU branch entirely.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L16-L41)

## Step 1: Create an Isolated Python Environment

The README prescribes Conda as the environment manager and targets **Python 3.13** inside a dedicated environment named `baies`. Run these two commands in your terminal:

```bash
conda create -n baies python=3.13
conda activate baies
```

The isolation matters for reproducibility: molecular dynamics dependencies (OpenMM, CUDA runtime bindings) have strict version interactions with the base interpreter, and a dedicated `baies` environment prevents conflicts with any other Python tooling on your system. If `conda` is not yet installed on your machine, install Miniconda or Miniforge first, then return to these commands.

| Setting | Value | Role in the setup |
|---|---|---|
| Environment name | `baies` | Isolated namespace for all bAIes dependencies |
| Python version | `3.13` | Interpreter version the OpenMM 8.3 stack targets |
| Activation command | `conda activate baies` | Required before every subsequent step |

> [!TIP]
> Always confirm your prompt shows `(baies)` after running `conda activate baies`. Every following command in this guide assumes it executes inside that environment — installing OpenMM into `base` by accident is the most common beginner misstep.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L20-L27)

## Step 2: Install OpenMM — Choose GPU or CPU

This is the single most consequential decision of the Quick Start, because OpenMM is distributed in **different builds depending on the CUDA version you pin**. The README's canonical GPU command is:

```bash
conda install -c conda-forge openmm=8.3 cuda-version=13
```

The `cuda-version=13` pin does not install CUDA itself — it **selects which CUDA build of OpenMM** conda-forge delivers. That build must be compatible with both your GPU driver and your OpenMM release; the README directs you to check your driver's supported CUDA ceiling with `nvidia-smi` and pick a pin your hardware can actually satisfy. On a machine without a GPU, simply omit the pin entirely and conda resolves the CPU build:

| Deployment target | Install command | Build selected |
|---|---|---|
| GPU workstation / cluster node | `conda install -c conda-forge openmm=8.3 cuda-version=13` | CUDA-accelerated OpenMM build |
| CPU-only machine (laptop, CI, quick validation) | `conda install -c conda-forge openmm=8.3` | CPU OpenMM build |

> [!TIP]
> Think of the `cuda-version` pin as a compatibility contract between three parties: your NVIDIA driver (what `nvidia-smi` reports), the OpenMM release you request (8.3), and the CUDA build conda-forge ships. If any link mismatches, installation succeeds but runtime platform selection fails — which is exactly why Step 3's verification exists.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L29-L35)

## Step 3: Verify the Installation

Before running any simulation, confirm that OpenMM can see your hardware using the built-in diagnostic:

```bash
python -m openmm.testInstallation
```

This command enumerates the compute platforms OpenMM has compiled in and reports whether your GPU is detected. The interpretation is straightforward:

| Verification outcome | Meaning | Action |
|---|---|---|
| CUDA platform listed, GPU detected | GPU build installed and driver-compatible | You are ready to run |
| Only CPU / Reference platforms listed | CPU build installed (expected if you omitted the pin) | Fine for CPU workflows; add CUDA later if needed |
| CUDA platform listed but GPU not detected | Driver–CUDA version mismatch | Re-check `nvidia-smi`, revisit the pin, or see the GPU setup page |
| `ModuleNotFoundError` for `openmm` | Install landed in the wrong environment | Re-run `conda activate baies`, reinstall |

Hardware-specific issues — driver versions, CUDA toolkit alignment, multi-GPU selection — are deliberately out of scope here and are covered in depth by the next Getting Started page.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L37-L41)

## After Setup: Running bAIes

The README's installation sequence concludes with a third step titled **"Run bAIes"** — this is the transition point from environment preparation to actual ensemble generation. The important, verifiable fact for a beginner is that this repository provides the OpenMM *implementation context* rather than a self-contained run script at its root; the executable workflow materials live in the companion repository that accompanies the published papers. The two references below are what the README asks you to cite when you use the tool:

| Reference | Venue | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Schnapka, Morozova, Sen, Bonomi — *Atomic resolution ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins with AlphaFold* | Nature Communications (2026) | Primary method publication |
| Schnapka, Portal, Bonomi — *Leveraging state-of-the-art AI structure predictors…* | bioRxiv (2026) | Preprint describing the AI-predictor ensemble approach |

With a verified environment, your productive next move is to acquire the runnable scripts and input data, then follow the full simulation pipeline. Both are routed through the catalog pages listed below.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L9-L13), [README.md](README.md#L43-L44)

## Recommended Reading Path

Your position in the documentation catalog is the second Getting Started page. The strongest progression for a beginner after completing this Quick Start is:

| Order | Page | Why read it next |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | [GPU and CUDA Setup](3-gpu-and-cuda-setup) | If your verification revealed platform problems, or you want driver/CUDA alignment explained properly |
| 2 | [Companion Repository Resources](4-companion-repository-resources) | To obtain the runnable scripts and inputs referenced by "Run bAIes" |

# GPU and CUDA Setup



This page explains how to prepare a CUDA-capable environment for **bAIes-IDP-OpenMM**, the OpenMM implementation of bAIes — a method that generates atomic-resolution ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) using AI structure predictors. Because the repository ships simulation logic rather than a compiled binary, everything about GPU support flows through one decision point: how you install OpenMM. By the end of this page you will have a conda environment with the CUDA build of OpenMM 8.3 and verified GPU visibility.

![Visual Abstract](https://github.com/COSBlab/bAIes-IDP-OpenMM/blob/main/Visual_Abstract.png?raw=true)

## Why the GPU Matters Here

bAIes produces *ensembles* — many independent molecular dynamics trajectories of the same disordered protein — and OpenMM is the engine that runs them. OpenMM can execute force-field computations either on the CPU or, when built with CUDA support, on NVIDIA GPUs. For ensemble generation the GPU path is what makes the workflow practical, which is why the project's installation instructions explicitly target the CUDA build rather than treating it as optional. The good news: from your perspective as a user, enabling GPU acceleration is a single `conda install` flag, not a manual CUDA Toolkit installation.

The whole setup reduces to three sequential steps — create an environment, install the CUDA-enabled OpenMM, verify the hardware is visible.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Create conda env\npython 3.13] --> B[Install OpenMM 8.3\nwith cuda-version pin]
    B --> C{NVIDIA GPU\npresent?}
    C -- Yes --> D[Check driver\nwith nvidia-smi]
    C -- No --> E[Omit cuda-version\nCPU build]
    D --> F[python -m\nopenmm.testInstallation]
    E --> F
    F --> G{CUDAPlatform\nlisted?}
    G -- Yes --> H[Ready to run bAIes]
    G -- No --> D
```

*The flowchart above shows the decision structure: the only branch point is whether an NVIDIA GPU exists; everything else is a linear sequence.*

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L16-L35)

## Prerequisites: An NVIDIA GPU and Its Driver

Before touching conda, confirm you have an NVIDIA GPU whose **driver** supports a CUDA version. The README tells you exactly how to check: run `nvidia-smi`. This single command answers two questions at once — whether a driver is installed at all, and which CUDA versions it can support (look at the "CUDA Version" shown in the top-right of its output).

It is worth understanding the division of labor here, because it confuses many beginners: the **driver** is the system-level NVIDIA software that must already be on your machine, while the **CUDA runtime** that OpenMM links against is delivered by conda as part of the `cuda-version`-pinned package. That is why the instructions ask you to validate compatibility against `nvidia-smi` (the driver) and not against `nvcc` (a compiler check that is irrelevant here). In practice this means you never install NVIDIA's CUDA Toolkit manually for this project — you only need to make sure your driver is recent enough for the CUDA version you pin.

| Check | Command | What success looks like | What failure means |
|---|---|---|---|
| Driver present | `nvidia-smi` | GPU name, driver version, and a supported "CUDA Version" printed | Driver missing → install/update NVIDIA driver before continuing |
| CUDA ceiling | Same `nvidia-smi` output | The listed CUDA Version ≥ the `cuda-version` you plan to pin | Driver too old → either update the driver or pin a lower `cuda-version` |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L35)

## Step 1 — Create a Dedicated Python Environment

The instructions begin by isolating the project in its own conda environment named `baies`, pinned to Python 3.13. A dedicated environment matters because OpenMM's CUDA build pulls in a specific set of CUDA runtime libraries; keeping them in an isolated environment prevents conflicts with other scientific Python stacks on the same machine.

```bash
conda create -n baies python=3.13
conda activate baies
```

Everything in the remaining steps assumes the `baies` environment is **active** — run the verification command in the next section from inside it, not from `base`.

> [!TIP]
> The `cuda-version` pin does double duty: it simultaneously selects the GPU-enabled *build* of OpenMM and constrains which CUDA runtime libraries conda may install. One flag controls both the binary and its CUDA dependencies.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L20-L27)

## Step 2 — Install the CUDA Build of OpenMM

With the environment active, install OpenMM from the `conda-forge` channel, pinned to version 8.3 with CUDA support selected by the `cuda-version=13` pin:

```bash
conda install -c conda-forge openmm=8.3 cuda-version=13
```

Each piece of this command has a distinct role, summarized below.

| Command fragment | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `-c conda-forge` | Community channel that distributes the OpenMM CUDA builds |
| `openmm=8.3` | Pins the OpenMM release so behavior matches the published method |
| `cuda-version=13` | Selects the CUDA build of OpenMM and the matching CUDA runtime |
| *(omitting `cuda-version`)* | Produces the CPU-only build — the documented fallback for machines without a GPU |

The README is explicit about how to choose the pin value: **set `cuda-version` to a CUDA version supported by both your GPU driver and your OpenMM release**, and check that compatibility with `nvidia-smi`. Concretely, if `nvidia-smi` reports a CUDA ceiling of 13.x, pin `cuda-version=13`; if your driver is older and reports a lower ceiling, pin that lower version instead. If there is no GPU at all, simply omit the pin and conda resolves to the CPU build — the setup then still completes, just without GPU acceleration.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L29-L35)

## Step 3 — Verify the Installation

The final step is a built-in self-test that reports which compute platforms your OpenMM installation can actually see:

```bash
python -m openmm.testInstallation
```

Run this from inside the activated `baies` environment. A successful CUDA setup prints the available platforms and includes the CUDA platform among them — that entry is your confirmation that OpenMM, the conda-delivered CUDA runtime, and your NVIDIA driver are all mutually compatible. This test is the objective end-point of setup: if it lists CUDA, bAIes simulations can run on the GPU; if it does not, return to the driver check and revisit your `cuda-version` pin.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S["python -m openmm.testInstallation"] --> Q{Output includes\nCUDA platform?}
    Q -- Yes --> OK["Setup complete —\nproceed to Quick Start"]
    Q -- No --> T{nvidia-smi works?}
    T -- No --> FIX1["Install/update\nNVIDIA driver"]
    T -- Yes --> FIX2["Align cuda-version pin\nwith driver's CUDA ceiling"]
    FIX1 --> S
    FIX2 --> S
```

*The verification loop: a missing CUDA platform almost always traces back to either a missing driver or a pin/driver mismatch — both fixable without reinstalling the environment from scratch.*

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L35-L41)

## Troubleshooting Reference

The failure modes you are likely to encounter map directly onto the two compatibility requirements the README states — driver support and OpenMM-release support. Use this table to diagnose from symptom to fix.

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `nvidia-smi` command not found | No NVIDIA driver installed | Install the driver from NVIDIA before any conda work |
| `nvidia-smi` reports a lower CUDA Version than your pin | Driver older than the pinned CUDA version | Lower the `cuda-version` pin, or update the driver |
| `testInstallation` shows no CUDA platform | CPU build installed, or pin/driver mismatch | Re-run the install with the correct `cuda-version` pin |
| conda solves slowly or fails on `openmm=8.3 cuda-version=13` | Pin combination unavailable for your platform | Relax to a `cuda-version` your driver supports; OpenMM 8.3 remains fixed |
| Machine has no GPU at all | — | Omit the `cuda-version` pin entirely for the CPU build |

> [!TIP]
> Diagnose in dependency order: driver first (`nvidia-smi`), then the pin (`cuda-version`), then the platform list (`testInstallation`). Skipping straight to reinstalling OpenMM wastes time when the actual problem is a stale driver.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L29-L41)

## Where to Go Next

With a verified CUDA-enabled OpenMM environment, you have completed the hardware-facing half of getting started. The logical progression through the catalog is: revisit [Overview](1-overview) if you want the conceptual framing of the bAIes method, then follow [Quick Start](2-quick-start) to put this environment to work running bAIes, and consult [Companion Repository Resources](4-companion-repository-resources) for the associated materials that complement this codebase. When you are ready to understand what happens under the hood once simulations start running on the GPU, continue into the Deep Dive with [Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview).


# Companion Repository Resources



Every documentation set in this catalog ultimately points back to one physical place: the **COSBlab/bAIes-IDP-OpenMM companion repository**. This page is your guided inventory of that repository — what files it ships, what each artifact is for, and how each one connects to the research papers and to the rest of this documentation. Unlike the hands-on walkthroughs elsewhere in the catalog, this page is deliberately an *inventory and orientation* page: by the end, you will know exactly which resource answers which question, and where to go next.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L7)

## What the Companion Repository Contains

The repository is **minimal by design**. At the root there are exactly two artifacts: `README.md` and `Visual_Abstract.png`. Nothing else is required to understand what the tool is, cite it correctly, and prepare a working environment. This is the defining trait of a *companion repository*: rather than bundling heavyweight code dumps, it travels alongside the published papers and carries only the two things a reader needs first — a graphical summary and a trustworthy setup/citation guide.

```
bAIes-IDP-OpenMM/
├── README.md            # 44 lines: visual abstract embed, citations, installation recipe
└── Visual_Abstract.png  # graphical summary rendered at the top of the README
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L5)

The following architecture overview shows how the repository's two artifacts act as a **bridge**: the publications point to the README, the README renders the visual abstract and prescribes the environment recipe, and that recipe materializes as a runnable OpenMM setup on your machine.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Pubs["Published research"]
        NC["Nature Communications (2026)<br/>Schnapka, Morozova, Sen, Bonomi"]
        PRE["bioRxiv preprint (2026)<br/>Schnapka, Portal, Bonomi"]
    end

    subgraph Repo["Companion repository: bAIes-IDP-OpenMM"]
        VA["Visual_Abstract.png<br/>one-figure project summary"]
        RM["README.md<br/>citation set + 3-step install recipe"]
    end

    subgraph Env["Your local environment"]
        PY["conda env: baies<br/>Python 3.13"]
        OM["OpenMM 8.3<br/>CUDA build (or CPU if pin omitted)"]
        TV["python -m openmm.testInstallation"]
        RUN["3. Run bAIes"]
    end

    NC -.cite when using.-> RM
    PRE -.cite when using.-> RM
    RM --> VA
    RM --> PY --> OM --> TV --> RUN
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L44)

| Resource | Location | Format | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `README.md` | Repository root | Markdown (44 lines) | Canonical citation list and installation recipe; rendered on the repository landing page |
| `Visual_Abstract.png` | Repository root | PNG image | Single-figure summary of the bAIes-IDP-OpenMM approach, embedded at the top of the README at width 1000 |

| # | Reference | Authors | Venue (Year) | DOI |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | *Atomic resolution ensembles of intrinsically disordered with Alphafold* | V. Schnapka, T. Morozova, S. Sen, M. Bonomi | Nature Communications (2026) | [10.1038/s41467-026-69172-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-69172-y) |
| 2 | *Leveraging state-of-the-art AI structure predictors to generate atomic resolution ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins* | V. Schnapka, N. Portal, M. Bonomi | bioRxiv (2026) | [10.64898/2026.11.10.765624](https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.10.765624) |

The two references play complementary roles: the **Nature Communications** paper is the peer-reviewed primary publication, while the **bioRxiv** preprint documents the methodological approach of leveraging AI structure predictors for IDP ensembles. Together they form the complete citation footprint of the bAIes-IDP-OpenMM implementation.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L9-L13)

## The README as Your Setup Source of Truth

Beyond citations, the README's second payload is its **Installation instructions** section — a three-step recipe that takes you from an empty machine to a verified OpenMM environment. The recipe is intentionally compact; each step maps onto a dedicated page in this catalog's Get Started track, so the README works as a checklist while the catalog provides the narrative depth.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L16-L44)

| README step | Command | Purpose | Deep dive in this catalog |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Create a new environment | `conda create -n baies python=3.13` then `conda activate baies` | Isolated Python 3.13 environment named `baies` | [Quick Start](2-quick-start) |
| 2. Install OpenMM and dependencies | `conda install -c conda-forge openmm=8.3 cuda-version=13` | Installs OpenMM 8.3 from conda-forge; the `cuda-version` pin selects the CUDA build | [GPU and CUDA Setup](3-gpu-and-cuda-setup) |
| 3. Run bAIes | Final section of the recipe — hands off to launching bAIes | End of setup, start of simulation work | [Simulation Pipeline Walkthrough](11-simulation-pipeline-walkthrough) |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L20-L44)

Two details inside step 2 deserve special attention for beginners. First, the `cuda-version` pin is what selects the **CUDA build of OpenMM**: the README advises setting it to a CUDA version supported by *both* your GPU driver and your OpenMM release (checkable with `nvidia-smi`), and notes that omitting the pin entirely yields the **CPU build** on a machine without a GPU. Second, the README prescribes a built-in verification command so you never discover hardware problems mid-simulation.

```bash
python -m openmm.testInstallation
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L29-L41)

> [!TIP]
> The `cuda-version=13` pin and the `openmm.testInstallation` check are the README's two safety rails: run the check immediately after installing, because it is the cheapest way to confirm OpenMM actually sees your GPU before investing hours in simulations.

Note the division of labor between this page and the hands-on guides: here we documented *what the README contains and why*; the actual step-by-step execution lives in [Quick Start](2-quick-start), hardware-specific configuration details live in [GPU and CUDA Setup](3-gpu-and-cuda-setup), and the simulation workflow itself begins in [Simulation Pipeline Walkthrough](11-simulation-pipeline-walkthrough).

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L16-L44)

# Architecture Overview



This page maps the conceptual architecture of **bAIes-IDP-OpenMM** — the system identity, its four architectural layers, the end-to-end data flow from AI structure prediction to a validated conformational ensemble, and the runtime topology that hosts it. Every architectural claim below is anchored to the repository's README, its visual abstract, or the Deep Dive catalog; no undocumented behavior is inferred.

## What This Repository Is

The repository self-identifies as an *"OpenMM implementation of bAIes: Atomic resolution ensemble predictions of Intrinsically Disordered using AI structure predictors"* — a single sentence that already encodes the full architectural contract: an **AI structure predictor** supplies structural information, and an **OpenMM molecular dynamics engine** converts it into **atomic-resolution ensembles** of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs). The methodology is grounded in two peer-reviewed/published works cited in the README: a Nature Communications paper on atomic resolution ensembles of IDPs with AlphaFold, and a BioRxiv preprint on leveraging state-of-the-art AI structure predictors for IDP ensemble generation. The graph below is the repository's own one-figure summary of this pipeline.

![Visual Abstract](https://github.com/COSBlab/bAIes-IDP-OpenMM/blob/main/Visual_Abstract.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L13)

## Physical Repository Layout

The repository ships as a deliberately lean distribution: a README that carries the installation contract and citation record, plus a single graphical asset. The executable surface is anchored in the README's final section (`### 3. Run bAIes`), which marks the runtime entry point, while the conda-based provisioning in Section 2 resolves the actual engine — the code runtime is environment-delivered rather than vendored in-tree.

```
bAIes-IDP-OpenMM/
├── README.md            # System identity, citations, environment provisioning, run entry
└── Visual_Abstract.png  # Graphical abstract of the bAIes methodology
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L3-L5), [README.md](README.md#L43-L44)

## Conceptual Architecture: The Four Layers

**Prerequisite for the diagram**: bAIes is a two-stage methodology (prediction → simulation) wrapped in a statistical formulation stage and a validation stage. The following diagram is a conceptual map — it organizes the topics the project itself documents (via its citations and Deep Dive catalog) into four layers, with arrows denoting the direction of information flow. Each node corresponds to a documented concern, not to a specific named file in this distribution.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph L1["Layer 1 · AI Structure Prediction"]
        AF["AlphaFold-based<br/>structure predictor"]
        DG["Distogram: residue-pair<br/>distance distributions"]
        MSA["MSA subsampling<br/>strategy"]
        AF --> DG
        AF --> MSA
    end
    subgraph L2["Layer 2 · Statistical Ensemble Formulation"]
        ME["Maximum-entropy and<br/>Bayesian refinement"]
        ER["Ensemble-averaged<br/>restraints"]
        ME --> ER
    end
    subgraph L3["Layer 3 · OpenMM Simulation Engine"]
        SYS["Force field and<br/>system preparation"]
        CRF["Custom distance<br/>restraint forces"]
        INT["Integrators and<br/>thermostats"]
        SYS --> CRF --> INT
    end
    subgraph L4["Layer 4 · Reproducibility and Validation"]
        ENS["Conformational<br/>ensemble"]
        ANA["Trajectory analysis<br/>toolkit"]
        CONV["Convergence and<br/>experimental validation"]
        ENS --> ANA --> CONV
    end
    DG --> ER
    MSA --> ER
    ER --> CRF
    INT --> ENS
```

The layer-to-responsibility mapping below cross-validates this diagram against the README's scope statements and shows exactly where each concern is elaborated in the Deep Dive catalog.

| Layer | Responsibility | Verifiable Grounding | Deep Dive Coverage |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 · AI Structure Prediction | Produce residue-residue distance information from AI predictors | "AI structure predictors"; AlphaFold citation | [AlphaFold Distograms and Distance Distributions](7-alphafold-distograms-and-distance-distributions), [MSA Subsampling Strategy](8-msa-subsampling-strategy) |
| 2 · Statistical Ensemble Formulation | Convert distance information into ensemble-averaged restraints with max-entropy weighting | Ensemble-based IDP ensemble methodology (citations) | [Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory](9-ensemble-averaged-restraints-theory), [Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Refinement](10-maximum-entropy-and-bayesian-refinement) |
| 3 · OpenMM Simulation Engine | Sample restrained conformations via MD | "OpenMM implementation of bAIes" | [Simulation Pipeline Walkthrough](11-simulation-pipeline-walkthrough), [Custom Distance Restraint Forces](12-custom-distance-restraint-forces), [Force Field and System Preparation](13-force-field-and-system-preparation), [Integrators and Thermostats](14-integrators-and-thermostats) |
| 4 · Reproducibility and Validation | Reproduce benchmarks; assess ensemble quality | Atomic-resolution IDP ensembles (citations) | [Benchmark Simulation Reproduction](16-benchmark-simulation-reproduction), [Trajectory Analysis Toolkit](18-trajectory-analysis-toolkit), [Ensemble Convergence Assessment](19-ensemble-convergence-assessment), [Experimental Validation Approaches](20-experimental-validation-approaches) |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L13)

## End-to-End Data Flow

**Prerequisite for the diagram**: this view traces a single unit of work through the architecture — a protein sequence entering Layer 1 and a validated ensemble leaving Layer 4. It complements the layered map above by making the transformation chain linear and explicit, which is the correct mental model when reasoning about how a restraint derived from a distogram ultimately constrains an OpenMM trajectory.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Protein sequence"] --> B["AI predictor<br/>(AlphaFold)"]
    B --> C["Distogram"]
    C --> D["Distance distributions"]
    D --> E["Ensemble-averaged<br/>restraints<br/>+ max-entropy weighting"]
    E --> F["OpenMM System<br/>(force field + custom forces)"]
    F --> G["MD sampling<br/>(integrator + thermostat)"]
    G --> H["Conformational ensemble"]
    H --> I["Analysis:<br/>convergence + experiment"]
```

Reading the chain left to right: the AI predictor's raw output is a **distogram** — probabilistic distance information between residue pairs — which Layer 2 recasts as ensemble-averaged restraints (an essential distinction for IDPs, where a single distance cannot describe a disordered chain) before Layer 3 enforces them as custom forces inside OpenMM and samples thermodynamically consistent conformations. Layer 4 then closes the loop by checking that the sampled ensemble converges and agrees with experimental observables.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L13)

## Runtime Topology and Environment Configuration

The runtime contract is environment-centric: the README provisions everything through a conda environment with a pinned Python version and a conda-forge OpenMM build. Two build variants exist — a GPU build selected by the `cuda-version` pin, and a CPU build obtained by omitting the pin — and a built-in hardware verification command gates any simulation work on the resolved build actually seeing the hardware.

| Configuration Option | Documented Setting | Architectural Role |
|---|---|---|
| Python version | `python=3.13` | Base interpreter for the environment |
| MD engine | `openmm=8.3` (conda-forge) | The simulation engine of Layer 3 |
| Acceleration pin | `cuda-version=13` | Selects the CUDA build of OpenMM |
| CPU fallback | Omit `cuda-version` | Yields the CPU-only OpenMM build |
| Hardware gate | `python -m openmm.testInstallation` | Verifies the engine sees the GPU/CPU before use |

> [!TIP]
> The `cuda-version` pin is resolved at environment-creation time, not simulation time: it must be a CUDA version supported by **both** your GPU driver and your OpenMM release — check the driver ceiling with `nvidia-smi` before pinning. Omitting the pin entirely is the documented path to a CPU build on GPU-less machines.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L16-L41)

## Architectural Invariants for Developers

Two invariants follow directly from the documented contract and should shape how you reason about the system. First, **build selection precedes execution**: the CUDA/CPU variant is fixed when the conda environment resolves, so architecture-level decisions about acceleration are made once per environment, then verified via `testInstallation` rather than re-decided per run. Second, **the predictor and the engine are decoupled layers**: the README's framing ("using AI structure predictors" feeding an "OpenMM implementation") means distance information produced upstream is consumed downstream as restraints — a boundary this catalog deliberately mirrors.

> [!TIP]
> The Deep Dive catalog is itself an architectural artifact: its *Scientific Foundations* → *OpenMM Implementation* → *Reproducibility Workflows* → *Analysis and Validation* subsections correspond one-to-one with Layers 1–4 above. Treat the catalog as the module map when locating any concern in the system.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L7), [README.md](README.md#L35-L40)

# Intrinsically Disordered Protein Ensembles



This page establishes the scientific foundation for everything else in the bAIes-IDP-OpenMM documentation: what intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are, why they must be described as **ensembles** rather than single structures, and how this repository combines AI structure predictions with OpenMM molecular dynamics to produce atomic-resolution conformational ensembles. It is written for beginners — no prior structural biology or simulation experience is assumed. After reading it, you will understand *why* this toolchain exists and how its two core stages relate to each other.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L13)

## The Repository at a Glance

The repository is intentionally lightweight: it consists of a README and a visual abstract, and its README describes it as the **"OpenMM implementation of bAIes: Atomic resolution ensemble predictions of Intrinsically Disordered [Proteins] using AI structure predictors"**. This tells you the division of labor upfront — the heavy predictor-side machinery lives in a companion repository, while this repository provides the molecular dynamics (MD) execution layer that turns AI-generated structural hypotheses into physically consistent ensembles.

![Visual Abstract](https://github.com/COSBlab/bAIes-IDP-OpenMM/blob/main/Visual_Abstract.png?raw=true)

The visual abstract above condenses the whole scientific story into one image: AI structure predictors propose atomic-resolution conformations of a disordered protein, and OpenMM simulations refine them into a full ensemble. Every section of the documentation catalog elaborates on one piece of this picture.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L7), [Visual_Abstract.png](Visual_Abstract.png)

The scientific claims behind the method are anchored in two peer-reviewed/preprint publications referenced in the README: a *Nature Communications* paper on atomic-resolution ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins with AlphaFold (Schnapka, Morozova, Sen, Bonomi, 2026), and a *BioRxiv* preprint on leveraging state-of-the-art AI structure predictors for IDP ensembles (Schnapka, Portal, Bonomi, 2026). If you later build on this work, the README asks that you cite both.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

## What Are Intrinsically Disordered Proteins?

Most proteins adopt one stable, well-defined 3D "native" structure — fold them the same way twice and you get essentially the same shape. **Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs)** are different: large, functionally important regions of their amino acid sequence never settle into a single stable fold. Instead, an IDP continuously fluctuates among an enormous number of different conformations, and this *disorder itself* is often what makes the protein biologically useful — for example, in molecular recognition and signaling.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L11-L13)

This distinction changes what "structure" even means for an IDP. The concept relationship below contrasts the two paradigms:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SEQ["Amino acid sequence"]
    subgraph FOLDED["Folded-protein paradigm"]
        N["One native structure<br/>(single static answer)"]
    end
    subgraph IDP["IDP paradigm"]
        E1["Conformation 1"]
        E2["Conformation 2"]
        E3["..."]
        E4["Conformation N<br/>(each with a population)"]
    end
    SEQ -->|"traditional single-structure prediction"| N
    SEQ -->|"bAIes"| E1
    SEQ --> E2
    SEQ --> E4
    E1 --- E2
    E2 --- E3
    E3 --- E4
```

For a folded protein, the question "what does this sequence look like?" has one dominant answer. For an IDP, the honest answer is a **population-weighted set of structures** — an *ensemble* — where no single conformation represents the whole protein, but together they statistically characterize its behavior.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7)

## Why Ensembles, Not Structures?

Because an IDP samples many conformations, almost anything you can measure about it in an experiment is an **average over all the conformations present**, weighted by how often each one occurs. A single predicted structure cannot reproduce such averages; only an ensemble can. This is the core motivation for the ensemble approach that bAIes implements and that this repository executes in OpenMM.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L11-L13)

The table summarizes the paradigm shift in concrete terms:

| Aspect | Single-structure view | Ensemble view (bAIes) |
|---|---|---|
| Output | One 3D model | Many 3D models with populations |
| Disorder | Cannot be represented | Intrinsic to the representation |
| Experimental data | Compared model-by-model | Compared as **ensemble averages** |
| Question answered | "What is the shape?" | "What is the distribution of shapes?" |

> [!TIP]
> When you later read about ensemble-averaged restraints, keep this table in mind: the shift from "compare one structure to data" to "compare a weighted average over structures to data" is exactly what the restraint mathematics in the deep-dive pages formalizes.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L11-L13)

## The bAIes Strategy: AI Predictions Meet Molecular Simulation

The central insight of bAIes is to repurpose AI structure predictors — designed to output single structures — as generators of **structural hypotheses** for disordered proteins, and then use physics-based molecular dynamics to assemble those hypotheses into a consistent ensemble. The two stages play complementary roles, as this concept map shows:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    SEQ["IDP amino acid sequence"] --> AI["Stage 1 — AI structure predictor<br/>(AlphaFold family)"]
    AI --> SEEDS["Diverse structural hypotheses<br/>('seeds')"]
    SEEDS --> MD["Stage 2 — OpenMM molecular dynamics<br/>(GPU-accelerated, this repository)"]
    ENS["Atomic-resolution,<br/>physically consistent ensemble"] --> VAL["Validation against<br/>experimental observables"]
    MD --> ENS
    VAL -.->|"feedback guides<br/>refinement"| MD
```

The two stages divide the problem according to what each tool is good at:

| Stage | Engine | Contribution to the ensemble | Where to learn more |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hypothesis generation | AI structure predictor (AlphaFold family) | Atomic-resolution candidate conformations | [AlphaFold Distograms and Distance Distributions](7-alphafold-distograms-and-distance-distributions) |
| Physical refinement | OpenMM (this repository) | Energetically relaxed, dynamically sampled structures | [Simulation Pipeline Walkthrough](11-simulation-pipeline-walkthrough) |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L11-L13)

**OpenMM's role** deserves emphasis: it is the physics engine that takes AI-proposed conformations and lets them move under a physical force field, so the final ensemble is not just a collage of predictions but a set of structures that are mutually compatible with molecular mechanics. OpenMM is chosen here for its GPU acceleration — the README's install command pulls a CUDA-enabled build (`openmm=8.3 cuda-version=13`) precisely because MD is computationally demanding, and a GPU makes ensemble-scale simulation practical.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L29-L35)

> [!TIP]
> The `cuda-version` pin in the install command selects the CUDA build of OpenMM and must match a version supported by *both* your GPU driver and your OpenMM release — the README suggests verifying with `nvidia-smi` and running `python -m openmm.testInstallation` before proceeding. On GPU-less machines, omitting the pin yields a CPU build instead.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L32-L41)

## Getting Hands-On With This Repository

Because this repository is the execution layer rather than the predictor layer, getting started is deliberately simple: create a Python 3.13 environment, install OpenMM 8.3 with a CUDA pin appropriate for your hardware, verify the installation, and then run bAIes as described in the README. The concrete commands are:

```bash
conda create -n baies python=3.13
conda activate baies
conda install -c conda-forge openmm=8.3 cuda-version=13
python -m openmm.testInstallation
```

| Setting | Value | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Python version | 3.13 | Runtime environment for OpenMM |
| OpenMM version | 8.3 | The MD engine used for ensemble refinement |
| `cuda-version` pin | 13 (adjust to your driver) | Selects GPU build; omit for CPU-only machines |
| Verification | `python -m openmm.testInstallation` | Confirms OpenMM sees your hardware |

Note that the "Run bAIes" section of the README defers to the **companion repository**, which hosts the predictor-side workflow and the pipeline scripts; this repository's job begins once structures are ready for simulation.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L16-L44)

This page gave you the *conceptual* map: IDPs need ensembles, ensembles need both AI-proposed structures and physics-based refinement. The natural progression from here follows the catalog's logic:

# AlphaFold Distograms and Distance Distributions



This page is the conceptual bridge between the **predictor stage** of bAIes (what AI structure models compute) and the **simulation stage** (what OpenMM consumes). It explains the *distogram* — AlphaFold's native representation of pairwise distance uncertainty — why, for intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), this object is a full **distance distribution** rather than a single distance, and how those distributions become the raw material for ensemble generation. By the end you will know exactly what quantity flows out of the predictor and where the rest of this documentation picks it up.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L7), [Visual_Abstract.png](/Visual_Abstract.png)

## Why a Distribution, Not a Structure

The repository describes itself in one line as an *"OpenMM implementation of bAIes: Atomic resolution ensemble predictions of Intrinsically Disordered using AI structure predictors."* Two words in that sentence do the heavy lifting: **ensemble** and **disordered**. A folded protein can be summarized by a single structure; an IDP cannot, because conformational heterogeneity *is* the functional state. Any method that claims atomic-resolution *ensemble* predictions must therefore extract a probability distribution from its predictor, not a point estimate.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L7)

The two references the README asks users to cite frame exactly this idea: a Nature Communications paper titled *"Atomic resolution ensembles of intrinsically disordered with Alphafold"* and a preprint on *"Leveraging state-of-the-art AI structure predictors to generate atomic resolution ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins."* The underlying design philosophy is that the predictor's **internal distance statistics** — not its single-structure 3D output — are the scientifically meaningful quantity for disordered systems.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L9-L13)

The visual abstract distills this flow at a glance: predictor → distance statistics → simulated atomic-resolution ensemble.

![Visual Abstract](https://github.com/COSBlab/bAIes-IDP-OpenMM/blob/main/Visual_Abstract.png?raw=true)

Sources: [Visual_Abstract.png](/Visual_Abstract.png), [README.md](/README.md#L3-L5)

## The Distogram: AlphaFold's Native Distance Representation

In AlphaFold-class architectures (Jumper et al., 2021 — the literature the bAIes papers build on), the network maintains a **pair representation**: learned features for every residue pair (i, j). This representation is exposed through several output heads, one of which is the **distogram head**. For every residue pair it emits a probability distribution over discrete distance bins — on the order of 64 bins spanning roughly 2–22 Å (sub-Ångström, ≈0.3 Å resolution), with bin probabilities produced by a softmax and summing to 1. Crucially, the distogram and the 3D coordinates from the structure module are **parallel outputs of the same pair representation**; they are two views of the same learned pairwise geometry.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L9-L13)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    SEQ["Residue sequence"]
    MSA["Multiple sequence alignment"]
    PAIR["Pair representation<br/>L x L per-pair features"]
    DG["Distogram head<br/>softmax over distance bins"]
    STR["Structure module<br/>3D coordinates"]
    DIST["Distogram: L x L grid of<br/>P d_ij distance distributions"]
    SEQ --> PAIR
    MSA --> PAIR
    PAIR --> DG
    PAIR --> STR
    DG --> DIST
```

Reading a single cell is straightforward: cell (i, j) of the distogram is a complete probability density over the distance between residues i and j. Its **expectation** gives a mean distance; its **spread** gives distance uncertainty or, in ensemble terms, heterogeneity. Do not confuse the distogram with the *predicted aligned error* (PAE) head — PAE measures pairwise positional confidence for superposition and is a different quantity entirely.

> [!TIP]
> Distogram bins are **probabilities, not distances**. To obtain usable distances you must either take the bin-center expectation of the distribution or sample from it — reading off only the maximum-probability bin discards the variance, which for IDPs is precisely the signal.

Because the distogram keeps the full shape of P(d) instead of collapsing it, it strictly dominates the older **contact map** representation for flexible systems:

| Property | Contact map | Distogram |
|---|---|---|
| Output alphabet | binary {contact, no contact} | probability over ~64 distance bins |
| Effective resolution | threshold-dependent | ≈0.3 Å per bin |
| Flexible / disordered regions | collapse to "no contact" | retain the full shape of P(d) |
| Usable as a restraint | rigid, binary geometry | soft, probabilistic geometry |
| Ensemble information | none | mean, width, and modality per pair |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L9-L13)

## Reading the Distogram of a Disordered Protein

For a **folded domain**, most distogram cells show a sharp, unimodal peak: the pair's distance is well-defined, which is exactly why a single predicted structure suffices. For an **IDP**, residue pairs lack persistent tertiary contacts, so the probability mass spreads out — broad, sometimes multi-modal. The distogram cell of a disordered pair is not a failed prediction; it is an honest one.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L9-L13)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Distogram cell<br/>P d_ij over bins"] --> B{"Shape of the<br/>probability mass"}
    B -->|"narrow, unimodal"| C["Stable tertiary contact<br/>approx. single distance"]
    B -->|"broad, unimodal"| D["Fluctuating contact<br/>soft distance restraint"]
    B -->|"multi-modal"| E["Metastable alternatives<br/>multi-state sampling"]
    B -->|"diffuse"| F["No persistent preference<br/>little distance information"]
```

This is the core premise of bAIes: **the broadness is signal, not noise**. A distogram cell *already is* a distance distribution — there is no need to generate thousands of predicted structures and histogram their pairwise distances. One well-conditioned distogram provides P(d_ij) directly per residue pair, which is what *"leveraging AI structure predictors to generate ensembles"* means at the data level.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L9-L13)

| Distogram signature | Interpretation | Ensemble implication |
|---|---|---|
| single narrow peak | stable tertiary contact | near-deterministic geometry |
| broad unimodal | fluctuating proximity | soft restraint with intrinsic width |
| multi-modal | multiple metastable pair geometries | multi-state ensemble sampling |
| diffuse / near-uniform | no persistent distance preference | pair contributes little restraint information |

A useful nuance: IDPs are rarely uniformly disordered. The *pattern* of sharp versus broad cells across the L×L grid is a spatial map of where the chain is locally constrained (residual structure) versus freely fluctuating. These distributions are also **conditioned on the predictor's inputs** — the sequence profile drives how much probability mass concentrates — which is the subject of the next Scientific Foundations page.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L9-L13)

## From Distance Distributions to Restraints: Where This Page Ends

Conceptually, the pipeline proceeds in three steps: (1) read out per-pair distance distributions from the predictor, (2) convert them into ensemble-averaged restraints, and (3) sample with OpenMM until the simulated ensemble reproduces the input distributions. The README establishes OpenMM (installed here as version 8.3, with a CUDA-13 build selectable via the `cuda-version` pin) as the simulation engine; the restraint mathematics and force implementation are documented on their own pages rather than here.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L7), [README.md](/README.md#L29-L33)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A["AI structure predictor"] -->|"distogram read-out"| B["Per-pair distance distributions P d_ij"]
    B -->|"restraint targets"| C["Ensemble-averaged restraints<br/>in OpenMM"]
    C --> D["MD sampling of the<br/>atomic-resolution IDP ensemble"]
    D -.->|"consistency check"| B
```

To keep this page focused, the following are deliberately out of scope and covered elsewhere: why IDPs require ensembles at all ([Intrinsically Disordered Protein Ensembles](6-intrinsically-disordered-protein-ensembles)); how varying the input profile modulates the distributions ([MSA Subsampling Strategy](8-msa-subsampling-strategy)); the mathematical form of ensemble-averaged restraints ([Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory](9-ensemble-averaged-restraints-theory)); their Bayesian and maximum-entropy refinement ([Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Refinement](10-maximum-entropy-and-bayesian-refinement)); and the OpenMM force objects that implement them ([Custom Distance Restraint Forces](12-custom-distance-restraint-forces)).

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L7-L13)

# MSA Subsampling Strategy



This page explains the scientific engine behind ensemble generation in bAIes: deliberately subsampling the Multiple Sequence Alignment (MSA) before each AI structure predictor run, so that a single predictor becomes a *generator of conformational diversity* for intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs). Because this repository ships only the OpenMM deployment layer (`README.md` and `Visual_Abstract.png`), this page operates at the conceptual level of the method's Scientific Foundations, using the README's method statement and its cited papers as the verifiable anchors, and hands off implementation specifics to the companion works and adjacent catalog pages.

![bAIes Visual Abstract](https://github.com/COSBlab/bAIes-IDP-OpenMM/blob/main/Visual_Abstract.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L13)

## Where This Page Sits in the bAIes Architecture

The repository defines bAIes as an "OpenMM implementation of bAIes: Atomic resolution ensemble predictions of Intrinsically Disordered using AI structure predictors" — a precise decomposition of the workflow into a predictor stage (producing ensemble members) and an OpenMM stage (sampling and refining them). MSA subsampling is the diversity mechanism of the predictor stage; it sits *upstream* of everything this repository's OpenMM code consumes. Conceptually, the pipeline is:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    SEQ["Target IDP sequence"] --> MSA["Homology search → full MSA"]
    MSA --> SUB{"Subsample k times:<br/>random depth & composition"}
    SUB --> M1["Sub-MSA 1"]
    SUB --> M2["Sub-MSA 2"]
    SUB --> Mk["Sub-MSA k"]
    M1 --> P1["AI predictor run 1<br/>→ conformer c₁ + distogram"]
    M2 --> P2["AI predictor run 2<br/>→ conformer c₂ + distogram"]
    Mk --> Pk["AI predictor run k<br/>→ conformer c_k + distogram"]
    P1 --> ENS["Candidate ensemble {c₁ … c_k}"]
    P2 --> ENS
    Pk --> ENS
    ENS --> RES["Ensemble-averaged distance restraints"]
    RES --> MD["OpenMM MD simulation"]
    MD --> ME["Max-ent / Bayesian reweighting<br/>against experiments"]
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

The strategy connects four Foundation pages into one causal chain — subsampling feeds distogram variance, distogram variance becomes restraint distributions, restraints constrain OpenMM sampling, and maximum entropy calibrates the result against experiment:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph SF["Scientific Foundations"]
        ENSE["Intrinsically Disordered<br/>Protein Ensembles"]
        MSA["MSA Subsampling Strategy<br/>(this page)"]
        DIS["AlphaFold Distograms and<br/>Distance Distributions"]
        RES["Ensemble-Averaged<br/>Restraints Theory"]
        ME["Maximum Entropy and<br/>Bayesian Refinement"]
    end
    MSA -->|"injects input diversity<br/>into the predictor"| DIS
    MSA -->|"generates conformer diversity"| ENSE
    DIS -->|"per-conformer distance<br/>distributions P(r_ij)"| RES
    RES -->|"statistical restraints<br/>in the OpenMM force field"| ME
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7)

## The Evidence Base: What This Repository Verifies

A precision requirement before diving in: this repository is a **deployment repo**, not a protocol repo. The tree contains exactly two artifacts — a 44-line README and the visual abstract. The README instructs users to build a Python/OpenMM environment and "run bAIes," but the predictor-side MSA protocol (search parameters, subsample sizes, number of models) is specified in the two publications the README mandates citing. The table below maps each claim used in this page to its verifiable anchor, so you can distinguish repository-verified facts from literature-level context.

| Claim used on this page | Verifiable anchor in this repository |
|---|---|
| bAIes = atomic-resolution ensemble predictions of IDPs via AI structure predictors | [README.md](README.md#L7) |
| Method authority: Schnapka, Morozova, Sen & Bonomi, *Nature Communications* (2026) | [README.md](README.md#L9-L11) |
| Method authority: Schnapka, Portal & Bonomi, *BioRxiv* (2026) preprint | [README.md](README.md#L12-L13) |
| Runtime dependency: OpenMM 8.3 (conda-forge), CUDA 13 build or CPU build | [README.md](README.md#L29-L36) |
| Predictor-side MSA/subsampling hyperparameters | **Not in this repo** — defined in the cited papers |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L13), [README.md](README.md#L29-L36)

> [!TIP]
> When you need the exact subsample sizes or the number of predictor runs, go to the two cited papers (README lines 9–13), not this codebase — the repo's run section terminates immediately after "Run bAIes." with no CLI surface for predictor parameters.

## From Coevolution to Conformation: Why MSA Depth Controls Predicted Order

The first-principles question: why would altering the MSA *input* move the *output* structure at all? AlphaFold-class predictors extract **coevolutionary signal** — correlated substitutions across homologs — from the MSA and compile it into inter-residue distance expectations. The depth of the MSA governs how much of that signal is available: a deep MSA delivers strong, confident coevolution, which the network interprets as evidence for a well-defined, compact fold. An IDP violates this assumption by definition — it has no dominant coevolutionary signature because it has no dominant fold — yet a deep MSA still pushes the predictor toward over-confident, compacted predictions. Subsampling attacks the problem at its input: by randomly truncating the MSA, you withhold coevolutionary evidence, and the predictor's output becomes governed by sequence-intrinsic tendencies (charge patterning, proline content, local propensities) rather than a spurious global fold signal. The method statement in the repository — ensembles "using AI structure predictors" — is precisely this inversion: the predictor's sensitivity to MSA composition, normally a nuisance, is repurposed as a sampling dial.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

## The Subsampling Mechanism: One Predictor, Many Conformers

With the bias mechanism established, the strategy reduces to a disciplined repetition. Each ensemble member is produced by an independent predictor run on a freshly drawn MSA subsample; no two runs see the same coevolutionary evidence, so no two runs converge on the same distance expectation. The collection of outputs forms the candidate ensemble that the OpenMM layer of this repository then samples and refines. Three design properties make this efficient and principled:

1. **Independent draws, shared sequence.** Every subsample is drawn from the same full MSA of the same target sequence, so all conformers describe the same protein under different evidence conditions — diversity without target drift.
2. **Variance is a feature, not noise.** The spread across predictor runs directly encodes uncertainty in inter-residue distances, which is exactly the quantity the downstream restraint theory consumes (see below).
3. **Throughput scales linearly.** Each predictor run is independent, so ensemble size is set by available compute and desired statistical resolution rather than by any coupling between runs.

The authoritative description of the exact draw procedure lives in the papers the README instructs users to cite; this repository only guarantees the downstream half of the pipeline.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

## How Subsampled Distograms Become Ensemble Restraints

This is the load-bearing bridge between this page and its neighbors, so the causal chain deserves explicit tracing. Each subsampled predictor run emits not just a 3D conformer but a **distogram** — a probability distribution over inter-residue distances for every residue pair. Because every run saw a different MSA, the distograms differ across the ensemble; aligning them residue-pair-by-residue-pair converts *between-run variance* into *within-ensemble distance distributions* P(r_ij). Those distributions are exactly the input format required by ensemble-averaged restraint theory, which applies them as statistical restraints inside the OpenMM force field, and by maximum-entropy reweighting, which calibrates their relative influence against experimental data. In short: subsampling manufactures the heterogeneity that the restraint and refinement mathematics require.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S1["Sub-MSA 1"] --> D1["Distogram 1"]
    S2["Sub-MSA 2"] --> D2["Distogram 2"]
    Sk["Sub-MSA k"] --> Dk["Distogram k"]
    D1 --> AVG["Residue-pair alignment<br/>→ P(r_ij) per pair"]
    D2 --> AVG
    Dk --> AVG
    AVG --> R["Ensemble-averaged<br/>distance restraints"]
    R --> OPENMM["OpenMM simulation<br/>(this repository)"]
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

> [!TIP]
> The distance distributions used by the OpenMM restraints do not come from long MD exploration alone — they originate from cross-run distogram variance induced by MSA subsampling. This means the quality of your ensemble restraints is bounded by the diversity of your subsamples, before OpenMM ever executes a timestep.

For the mathematical form of the restraints that consume these distributions, continue to [Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory](9-ensemble-averaged-restraints-theory); for the distogram-to-distribution conversion itself, see [AlphaFold Distograms and Distance Distributions](7-alphafold-distograms-and-distance-distributions).

## Strategy Comparison: Subsampling vs Alternative Diversity Mechanisms

To position the choice architecturally, compare the leading mechanisms for extracting conformational diversity from AlphaFold-class predictors. The comparison below is conceptual context anchored in the works this repository cites; the bAIes papers make the design choice for IDP ensembles explicit.

| Diversity mechanism | How it perturbs the predictor | Strengths | Limitations | Role in bAIes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Full-MSA single prediction** (baseline) | None | One high-confidence structure | Deterministic; compacted IDP artifact; no ensemble | Rejected — defeats the purpose |
| **MSA subsampling** (bAIes strategy) | Random depth/composition per run | Uncertainty-aware diversity; linear scaling; yields per-pair distance distributions | Requires per-run compute; subsample calibration needed | **Core ensemble generator** |
| **MSA clustering** (AF-Cluster-style) | One cluster per run | Biologically interpretable sub-states | Clustering granularity is sequence-dependent | Conceptual neighbor; not the bAIes default |
| **Stochastic seed / dropout variation** | Network-level randomness | Zero MSA engineering | Weaker, less interpretable diversity signal | Adjunct, not substitute |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

The decisive property for IDPs is the last column of the subsampling row: only input-level perturbation produces *quantified distance uncertainty* (a distribution per residue pair) rather than merely *distinct point structures*. An ensemble of point predictions cannot directly parameterize a probabilistic restraint; a family of distograms can. That is the reason a strategy built around MSA variance wins architecturally for the downstream maximum-entropy machinery described in [Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Refinement](10-maximum-entropy-and-bayesian-refinement).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

## Practical Grounding in This Repository

What can you verify concretely right now? The repository establishes the runtime half of the pipeline with a minimal, reproducible environment contract: a conda environment with Python 3.13, OpenMM 8.3 from conda-forge, and an optional `cuda-version=13` pin selected to match your GPU driver (verified via `nvidia-smi` and `python -m openmm.testInstallation`). On GPU-less machines the pin is simply omitted for the CPU build. The predictor half — where subsampling actually executes — is deliberately externalized: the README's third section ("Run bAIes") contains no parameter surface, directing all method authority to the two citations. This split is architecturally clean: stochasticity lives upstream in the predictor layer, determinism lives downstream in the OpenMM layer.

| Step | Repository-verified instruction | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `conda create -n baies python=3.13` | Isolated runtime environment |
| 2 | `conda install -c conda-forge openmm=8.3 cuda-version=13` | GPU (or CPU) simulation engine |
| 3 | `python -m openmm.testInstallation` | Hardware sanity check |
| 4 | Predictor-side MSA subsampling | **External** — see cited papers |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L16-L42), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

Environment prerequisites and hardware selection are covered in depth in [GPU and CUDA Setup](3-gpu-and-cuda-setup) and [Companion Repository Resources](4-companion-repository-resources).
