# Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory



This page explains the theoretical foundation of bAIes: the decision to restrain **ensemble averages** rather than individual conformations. It covers the statistical argument for averaging, the mathematical formulation and its gradient, the flow of information from AI-predicted distance statistics into restraint targets, and the properties and trade-offs that follow. Implementation mechanics are deliberately out of scope here — they live in [Custom Distance Restraint Forces](12-custom-distance-restraint-forces) — and the probabilistic justification of restraint weights is developed in [Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Refinement](10-maximum-entropy-and-bayesian-refinement).

bAIes is defined in the repository as an "OpenMM implementation of bAIes: Atomic resolution ensemble predictions of Intrinsically Disordered using AI structure predictors" — note that *ensemble* is the operative word in the method's own one-line definition. The formalism below is the one described by the two publications the repository asks users to cite.

![Visual Abstract](https://github.com/COSBlab/bAIes-IDP-OpenMM/blob/main/Visual_Abstract.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L3-L5), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

## The Statistical Mismatch: Why One Structure Cannot Absorb Ensemble Data

AlphaFold-style predictors do not output a single truth for an intrinsically disordered protein (IDP); they output *statistics over conformational space* — most prominently the distogram, a per-residue-pair probability distribution over distances. For a folded protein these distributions are sharp enough that one conformation can satisfy nearly all of them simultaneously. For an IDP they are broad and mutually inconsistent by construction: a disordered chain's contact map says "these pairs are sometimes close, in different structures, at different times." If you convert those predictions into per-conformation distance restraints, every generated structure is forced to satisfy *all* predicted contacts *at once*. The result is a population of collapsed, frustrated conformers — structures that satisfy the data statistically but represent no member of the true underlying ensemble.

bAIes resolves this by relocating the statistical obligation from the individual structure to the population: the simulation must reproduce the predicted distances *on average*, across all concurrently sampled conformations. This is not merely a numerical convenience — it aligns the semantics of the restraint with the semantics of the prediction. The predicted quantity describes a distribution; the restrained quantity describes a distribution; the mismatch between them is what drives sampling toward heterogeneous, physically consistent ensembles.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L11-L13)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph A["Paradigm 1 — single-conformation restraints"]
        direction TB
        T1["Predicted pair distances<br/>g_α^pred (ensemble-statistical)"] --> R1["Restraint on each structure:<br/>g_α(x) ≈ g_α^pred for every pair"]
        R1 --> F1["One conformer must satisfy<br/>hundreds of incompatible contacts"]
        F1 --> O1["Collapsed, frustrated,<br/>non-physical structures"]
    end
    subgraph B["Paradigm 2 — ensemble-averaged restraints (bAIes)"]
        direction TB
        T2["Predicted pair distances<br/>g_α^pred"] --> R2["Restraint on the population:<br/>⟨g_α⟩ ≈ g_α^pred"]
        R2 --> F2["Each conformer satisfies only<br/>a physically compatible subset"]
        F2 --> O2["Diverse, atomically resolved<br/>IDP ensemble"]
    end
```

The two paradigms differ in what entity is held accountable to the data:

| Dimension | Single-conformation restraints | Ensemble-averaged restraints (bAIes) |
|---|---|---|
| Restrained entity | Each individual structure | The population average ⟨g⟩ |
| Per-structure obligation | Satisfy all restraints simultaneously | Satisfy only a compatible subset |
| Effect on heterogeneity | Collapses ensemble variance | Preserves and shapes it |
| Failure mode | Frustrated, over-packed conformers | None of a single structure; bias shifts to ensemble level |
| Data semantics matched | Treats distributional data as deterministic | Matches distribution-to-distribution |
| Suitable input | Experimentally resolved single structures | Predictor statistics (distograms), ensemble experiments |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

## The Mathematical Formulation

The formalism operates on $N$ conformations $x_1, \dots, x_N$ simulated concurrently, each carrying the physical force field energy $E_{\mathrm{ff}}(x_k)$. For each restrained quantity — indexed $\alpha$, in practice one per atom pair $(i,j)$ — the predictor supplies a target value $g^{\mathrm{pred}}_\alpha$, and the simulation supplies an instantaneous observable $g_\alpha(x_k)$ measured on every replica. The ensemble average of the observable is

$$\langle g_\alpha \rangle \;=\; \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=1}^{N} g_\alpha(x_k)$$

and the restraint contributes the following term to the total energy of the coupled system:

$$E_{\mathrm{total}} \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{N} E_{\mathrm{ff}}(x_k) \;+\; \frac{\omega}{2} \sum_{\alpha} \Big( \langle g_\alpha \rangle - g^{\mathrm{pred}}_\alpha \Big)^{2}$$

The only new object compared to standard MD is the second term: a harmonic penalty on the *deviation between the ensemble average and the predicted target*, scaled by a strength $\omega$. Everything about the method's behavior — its self-regulation, its effect on heterogeneity, its numerical requirements — follows from differentiating this term.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

The gradient distributes the ensemble-level penalty back onto individual replicas:

$$\frac{\partial E_{\mathrm{total}}}{\partial x_k} \;=\; \nabla_{x_k} E_{\mathrm{ff}}(x_k) \;+\; \frac{\omega}{N} \sum_{\alpha} \Big( \langle g_\alpha \rangle - g^{\mathrm{pred}}_\alpha \Big) \, \nabla_{x_k}\, g_\alpha(x_k)$$

Two structural features of this expression carry the entire theory. First, the **$1/N$ prefactor**: each replica receives only a $1/N$ share of the ensemble deviation, because each replica contributes only a $1/N$ share of the average. Second, the **deviation factor** $\langle g_\alpha \rangle - g^{\mathrm{pred}}_\alpha$ is computed *globally* — it couples all replicas and is identical for every $k$. For a distance observable $g_\alpha(x) = |\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j|$, the inner gradient is simply the unit vector along the pair axis, so the ensemble deviation is converted into ordinary physical-looking forces whose magnitudes are set by population-level agreement rather than by the individual pair distance.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

The symbols used throughout this page:

| Symbol | Meaning | Role in the theory |
|---|---|---|
| $x_k$ | Coordinates of conformation $k$ | The trajectory being integrated |
| $N$ | Number of concurrent conformations | Ensemble size; sets the $1/N$ force scaling |
| $g_\alpha(x_k)$ | Instantaneous observable (e.g., pair distance) | Measured per replica per step |
| $\langle g_\alpha \rangle$ | Ensemble average of the observable | The quantity actually restrained |
| $g^{\mathrm{pred}}_\alpha$ | Predictor-derived target value | What the average must reproduce |
| $\Delta_\alpha = \langle g_\alpha \rangle - g^{\mathrm{pred}}_\alpha$ | Ensemble deviation | The global coupling signal |
| $\omega$ | Restraint strength | Trades target adherence against heterogeneity |
| $\nabla_{x_k} g_\alpha$ | Gradient of the observable | Converts deviation into per-atom forces |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7)

An exact algebraic identity makes the contrast between the paradigms quantitative. If you restrained each replica *individually* against the same target and averaged the resulting energies, you would obtain

$$\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N} \big(g_\alpha(x_k) - g^{\mathrm{pred}}_\alpha\big)^{2} \;=\; \big(\langle g_\alpha \rangle - g^{\mathrm{pred}}_\alpha\big)^{2} \;+\; \mathrm{Var}\big[g_\alpha\big]$$

Naive per-replica restraints therefore secretly restrain two things: the ensemble average **and** the ensemble variance — the second term actively punishes conformational spread. The bAIes restraint drops the variance term by design: heterogeneity is not tolerated as a cost, it is protected as the object of interest.

> [!TIP]
> The **vanishing-force property** is the mechanism that makes ensemble-averaged restraints self-regulating: once $\langle g_\alpha \rangle = g^{\mathrm{pred}}_\alpha$ for a restraint, its gradient contribution is exactly zero *for every replica simultaneously* — regardless of how far any individual structure's distance lies from the target. Individual violations carry no energetic penalty at the ensemble-consistent point, which is precisely what allows the ensemble to stay heterogeneous while matching predictor statistics.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

## From Predictor Output to Restraint Targets

The restraint theory consumes the predictor output at a well-defined boundary. Upstream, AlphaFold-style predictors produce a distogram — a probability distribution over distances for every residue pair — sharpened or diversified by the MSA information fed to the model. At the boundary, distogram statistics are distilled into concrete scalar targets $g^{\mathrm{pred}}_\alpha$ suitable for the harmonic formulation above. Downstream, OpenMM enforces agreement between the simulated ensemble average and those targets. The details of distogram interpretation belong to [AlphaFold Distograms and Distance Distributions](7-alphafold-distograms-and-distance-distributions), and the mechanism by which different MSA samples produce differently weighted, diversity-enhancing predictions belongs to [MSA Subsampling Strategy](8-msa-subsampling-strategy); here it suffices to note that both feed *distributional* information into targets that only make physical sense when restrained at the ensemble level — which is why the averaging formalism of the previous section is the load-bearing component of the method.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["AI structure predictor<br/>(distogram per residue pair)"] --> B["Target construction<br/>g_α^pred from predicted<br/>distance statistics"]
    B --> C["Ensemble-averaged restraint<br/>(ω/2) Σ_α (⟨g_α⟩ − g_α^pred)²"]
    C --> D["OpenMM MD engine<br/>force field + restraint gradient"]
    D --> E["Conformer population<br/>x_1 … x_N"]
    E -- "instantaneous observables g_α(x_k)" --> C
    B -. "diversity via MSA subsampling" .-> A
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7)

## Ensemble Feedback During Simulation

During the simulation, the restraint is not a static additive term — it is a closed feedback loop executed every MD step. Each replica's instantaneous observables are collected, the ensemble average is formed globally, the deviation from the predictor targets is computed once, and a $1/N$-scaled gradient is delivered back to every replica, where it is added to the force field forces and integrated under the thermostat. The ensemble deviation $\Delta_\alpha$ acts as a global control signal: when the population drifts toward too much contact (average too short), forces push pairs apart across the whole population; when the population drifts toward too little contact, forces pull pairs together. No single replica is ever told what to be — the population is told what to average.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant K as Replica k (k = 1…N)
    participant C as Ensemble coupling
    loop every MD step
        K->>C: instantaneous observables g_α(x_k)
        C->>C: ⟨g_α⟩ = (1/N) Σ_k g_α(x_k)
        C->>C: deviation Δ_α = ⟨g_α⟩ − g_α^pred
        C->>K: per-replica force (ω/N) Σ_α Δ_α ∇g_α(x_k)
        K->>K: integrate F_ff + F_restraint (thermostatted NVT)
    end
```

The loop's global coupling has a direct implementation consequence that the theory implies but does not concern itself with: replicas cannot evolve as fully independent simulations, because every step requires communication of observables to form the average and distribution of gradients back. How OpenMM realizes this cross-replica coupling is documented in [Custom Distance Restraint Forces](12-custom-distance-restraint-forces), and the thermostat choices governing the integration are covered in [Integrators and Thermostats](14-integrators-and-thermostats).

> [!TIP]
> The $1/N$ scaling cuts both ways. Statistically, the ensemble average estimated from finite replicas carries noise on the order of $\sigma/\sqrt{N}$, so a larger ensemble yields a quieter, more stable deviation signal and gentler restraint dynamics. Dynamically, however, each individual replica only ever feels a $1/N$ share of that signal — so increasing ensemble size stabilizes the *population* target-tracking while weakening the per-replica pull. Practical runs balance these effects jointly with $\omega$; validating that the population actually converged is the job of [Ensemble Convergence Assessment](19-ensemble-convergence-assessment).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

## Properties, Trade-offs, and Theoretical Guarantees

The formalism has a coherent profile of strengths and costs, summarized below.

| Property | Consequence | Practical implication |
|---|---|---|
| Distribution-to-distribution semantics | Predicted statistics are interpreted as statistics | Broad distograms yield broad ensembles, as intended |
| Vanishing-force at agreement | Zero restraint force once the average matches | Heterogeneity is preserved at the target point |
| Variance term excluded | Ensemble spread is not penalized | No artificial collapse; spread set by physics + targets |
| $1/N$ gradient scaling | Per-replica pull weakens with ensemble size | Population stability improves with $N$, per-replica influence drops |
| $\sqrt{N}$ averaging noise | Finite-ensemble deviation estimates fluctuate | Requires sufficient $N$ for a smooth control signal |
| Global deviation coupling | Replicas are coupled through $\Delta_\alpha$ | Simulation cost scales with $N$; replicas exchange information |
| Choice of $\omega$ | Single dial trading adherence vs. freedom | Under-restraining ignores data; over-restraining approaches the naive paradigm |
| Correlated restraints | Many pair targets are not independent | Ensemble deviation vectors interfere; effective strength is pair-dependent |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

The $\omega$ dial has a principled resolution beyond manual tuning. The harmonic-on-average energy can be re-derived as the outcome of a maximum-entropy inference problem: among all ensembles consistent with the predicted observables, the least-biased one is the one that stays maximally close to the physical prior (the force field alone) — and the resulting objective takes precisely the restrained-MD form, with $\omega$ fixed by the statistical weight of the data. This reframing also delivers a Bayesian reading, in which the restraint plays the role of a likelihood term over the ensemble. The full derivation and its refinement machinery are the subject of [Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Refinement](10-maximum-entropy-and-bayesian-refinement); the point to retain here is that the ensemble-average formulation is not one heuristic among several — it is the form that principled ensemble inference takes when operationalized as molecular dynamics.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

## Where This Fits in bAIes and What to Read Next

Within the bAIes chain — predictor statistics → restraint targets → ensemble MD → analysis and validation — this page is the hinge: it is the stage where *predictor* information, which describes distributions, is translated into *dynamical* forces, which act on coordinates. Everything downstream inherits its semantics from the averaging decision made here. The natural reading order out of this page follows the same information flow: continue to [Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Refinement](10-maximum-entropy-and-bayesian-refinement) for the principled justification of restraint weights, then to [Simulation Pipeline Walkthrough](11-simulation-pipeline-walkthrough) and [Custom Distance Restraint Forces](12-custom-distance-restraint-forces) to see the formalism executed in OpenMM, and finally to [Ensemble Convergence Assessment](19-ensemble-convergence-assessment) to verify that the produced population genuinely satisfies the theory's central promise — predictor statistics reproduced by a heterogeneous, atomically resolved ensemble.


# Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Refinement



This page documents the inference principle that binds the bAIes workflow together: given a prior ensemble generated from AI structure predictors and sparse, ensemble-averaged data, how do we produce the **least-biased refined posterior**? Previous pages established *where* the prior comes from ([Intrinsically Disordered Protein Ensembles](6-intrinsically-disordered-protein-ensembles), [AlphaFold Distograms and Distance Distributions](7-alphafold-distograms-and-distance-distributions), [MSA Subsampling Strategy](8-msa-subsampling-strategy)) and *what* is restrained ([Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory](9-ensemble-averaged-restraints-theory)). This page establishes *why the refinement rule itself is well-founded*.

The repository itself is intentionally lean—it hosts the OpenMM implementation entry point and the canonical visual abstract, with the scientific formalization carried by the two cited publications.

![Visual Abstract](https://github.com/COSBlab/bAIes-IDP-OpenMM/blob/main/Visual_Abstract.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L13), [Visual_Abstract.png](Visual_Abstract.png)

## The Inverse Problem: Why Ensembles Demand a Refinement Principle

Intrinsically disordered proteins occupy enormous conformational spaces, and the experimental observables available to characterize them are few and **ensemble-averaged**—a single measurement constrains a distribution over millions of conformations, not a single structure. This inverse problem is radically underdetermined: infinitely many ensembles match the data, and most of them are physically absurd in ways the data cannot detect. bAIes confronts this by supplying two independent information sources: a **generative prior** from AI structure predictors (AlphaFold-derived ensembles, diversified via MSA subsampling) and **data** in the form of ensemble-averaged distance restraints. The remaining question is purely one of inference: what update rule merges these sources without injecting bias that neither source justifies? Maximum entropy is that rule, and Bayesian refinement is its probabilistic restatement. This is precisely the framing under which bAIes is published—atomic-resolution IDP ensembles derived from AI predictors, with the inference machinery executed inside OpenMM simulations.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L13)

## The Maximum Entropy Solution: Least-Biased Updating

The maximum entropy principle selects, among all ensembles consistent with the data, the one closest to the prior in the Kullback–Leibler sense. Formally, we minimize `D_KL(P ‖ P₀)` subject to the moment conditions `⟨fₖ⟩_P = fₖ*`, where `P₀(x)` is the prior ensemble, `fₖ(x)` are the restrained observables, and `fₖ*` their target values. The analytic solution is an **exponential-family distribution**:

```
Maximum entropy form:
    P(x | D) ∝ P₀(x) · exp( −Σₖ λₖ · fₖ(x) )

with the Lagrange multipliers λₖ fixed by the constraints:
    ⟨fₖ⟩_P = fₖ*   for every restrained observable k
```

Three properties make this form operationally decisive. First, the posterior is the prior *modulated*—conformations that satisfy the restraints are upweighted, those that violate them are downweighted, and nothing else changes; no structural information enters beyond what the data demands. Second, the solution is parameterized entirely by the multipliers `λₖ`, so the entire refinement reduces to calibrating one scalar per observable. Third, `λₖ → 0` recovers the prior exactly, making the entropy term a built-in **regularizer against overfitting**: the weaker the restraint, the more the ensemble defaults to what the AI predictor believed before seeing any data. These properties are what distinguish principled refinement from ad-hoc reweighting, and they follow the formalization given in the cited bAIes publications.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

## The Bayesian Reading: Prior × Likelihood

The identical posterior emerges from a Bayesian treatment in which each ensemble-averaged observable carries a Gaussian likelihood whose width `σₖ` encodes experimental and model uncertainty:

```
Bayesian form:
    P(x | D) ∝ P₀(x) · exp( −Σₖ (⟨fₖ⟩ − fₖ*)² / (2σₖ²) )
```

The two formulations are **not alternatives but two coordinate systems on the same posterior**. In the maximum-entropy view, `λₖ` is a Lagrange multiplier and the data enter as hard moment constraints. In the Bayesian view, `λₖ` is implicitly calibrated by the inverse noise scale—noisier data (larger `σₖ`) produce weaker effective restraints—so the likelihood automatically implements the entropy term's regularizing behavior. The Bayesian reading adds two capabilities the pure MaxEnt view leaves implicit: an explicit home for **uncertainty modeling** (the `σₖ` parameters absorb experimental error and predictor error alike), and a route to **hyperparameter inference** through the marginal likelihood, which arbitrates between trusting the prior and trusting the data. For an advanced implementer, the practical consequence is that restraint tolerance and restraint strength are not independent knobs—they are two projections of the same inference calibration.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

## Equivalence Map: From Inference to OpenMM

The following concept diagram traces how the prior-generation machinery documented earlier in this catalog and the data channel converge into a single exponential-family posterior, shown in both inferential readings:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph PRIOR["Prior information - P0 of x"]
        direction TB
        AI["AI structure predictors<br/>AlphaFold distograms"]
        SUB["MSA subsampling<br/>conformational diversity"]
        FF["OpenMM force-field sampling"]
        AI --> SUB --> FF
    end
    subgraph DATA["Data information"]
        direction TB
        OBS["Ensemble-averaged target values fk-star"]
        NOISE["Uncertainty model sigma-k"]
    end
    subgraph UPDATE["Least-biased inference"]
        direction LR
        ME["Maximum entropy view:<br/>minimize D-KL of P vs P0<br/>subject to fk mean = target"]
        BAY["Bayesian view:<br/>posterior = prior × Gaussian likelihood<br/>width sigma-k"]
    end
    FF -->|"initial ensemble"| ME
    OBS --> ME
    NOISE --> BAY
    ME <-->|"identical exponential-family posterior"| BAY
    BAY --> POST["Refined posterior ensemble P of x given D"]
    ME --> POST
```

The table below is the operative translation layer for anyone implementing or auditing this pipeline—the left columns are inference quantities, the right column is where each lives in the bAIes execution model:

| Inference quantity | Maximum-entropy reading | Bayesian reading | bAIes realization |
|---|---|---|---|
| `P₀(x)` | Reference measure | Prior belief | AI-predictor ensemble (distograms + MSA subsampling) sampled under the force field |
| `fₖ(x)` | Constraint functional | Data-generating observable | Collective variable inside an ensemble-averaged custom restraint |
| `λₖ` | Lagrange multiplier | Strength calibrated by noise scale `σₖ` | Restraint force constant |
| `⟨fₖ⟩_P = fₖ*` | Moment-matching condition | Likelihood optimum | Equilibrium enforced by the ensemble-average restraint during dynamics |
| Entropy term `−D_KL(P‖P₀)` | Objective regularizer | Log prior density | Deviations decay back toward the AI prior when restraint strength relaxes |

The repository establishes the execution substrate for this mapping: bAIes runs as an OpenMM simulation, meaning the posterior is never evaluated analytically—it is *sampled*, with the exponential family realized as an energy landscape `U_total(x) = U_forcefield(x) + Σₖ λₖ fₖ(x)` explored at thermal equilibrium.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L13), [README.md](README.md#L16-L35)

> [!TIP]
> An ensemble-average restraint pushes every individual conformation as if it were the whole ensemble, yet its correctness is only defined by the running ensemble average. Never validate or tune such a restraint against a single frame—doing so silently converts a maximum-entropy ensemble refinement into an overfitting per-structure fit.

## The Refinement Loop in Practice

Because the posterior is an energy landscape, refinement in bAIes is an iterative sampling procedure rather than a closed-form calculation:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Prior ensemble<br/>from AI predictor + force field"] --> B["Attach ensemble-average restraints<br/>with initial strengths lambda-k"]
    B --> C["Run OpenMM dynamics<br/>multiple conformational copies"]
    C --> D["Measure running ensemble averages fk-mean"]
    D -->|"fk-mean not at targets"| E["Recalibrate lambda-k<br/>against noise scales sigma-k"]
    E --> C
    D -->|"fk-mean matches targets"| F["Sampled posterior:<br/>exponential-family ensemble"]
```

The calibration of `λₖ` (equivalently, the restraint force constants) constitutes a **thermodynamic path** from prior to posterior: at zero strength the simulation samples `P₀` exactly, and as strength rises the trajectory ensemble slides toward the data-consistent posterior. This path structure is what later pages exploit for quality control—restraint convergence and the sensitivity of derived observables to `λ` are the operational tests of whether the refinement is trustworthy. The procedural handoff is exact: this page supplies the *why* of the loop, while the mechanics of the custom forces that implement `fₖ(x)` inside OpenMM are documented in [Custom Distance Restraint Forces](12-custom-distance-restraint-forces) and the full execution sequence in [Simulation Pipeline Walkthrough](11-simulation-pipeline-walkthrough).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L16-L43)

> [!TIP]
> λ and σ are coupled, not independent: λ → 0 recovers the AI prior exactly, while raising λ without noise-aware calibration silently overfits to the restraint targets. The entropy term is your only structural guard—track the KL divergence of the running ensemble back to the prior throughout refinement.

## Strategy Comparison: Where bAIes Sits Among Ensemble-Refinement Approaches

The design choice embodied in bAIes is best understood by contrast. Each row is a legitimate strategy; the columns expose why ensemble-averaged Bayesian restraints dominate for IDPs, where ensemble variance is itself a physical observable:

| Strategy | What is constrained | Bias introduced | Overfitting risk | Fit for IDP ensembles |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Unbiased force-field MD | Nothing | Force-field bias only | None from data | Insufficient—sampling rarely converges on IDP scales |
| Per-conformation restraints | Each structure against data independently | Destroys ensemble variance; overcounts data by N copies | Severe | Poor—collapses the very heterogeneity under study |
| MaxEnt reweighting of fixed conformers | Weights only; conformers frozen | Minimal in weight space | Moderate | Limited—blind to states absent from the prior conformer pool |
| **Bayesian ensemble-averaged restraints (bAIes)** | Ensemble averages only | Minimal-biased update of a *generative sampler* | Controlled by noise model + entropy regularizer | Strong—variance remains dynamic, prior diversity is exploitable |

Two pros/cons axes deserve emphasis. **Pros** of the bAIes scheme: it preserves ensemble width as a sampled property rather than a fit parameter; it degrades gracefully to the AI prior under weak data; and every inferential quantity has a one-to-one force-level counterpart, making the method auditable inside a standard OpenMM run. **Cons**: correctness is inherited—if the prior or the force field is systematically wrong, the posterior cannot repair it; and restraint calibration inherits the uncertainty model, so a mis-set `σₖ` propagates directly into biased `λₖ`. These residual failure modes define exactly what the validation pages probe: [Ensemble Convergence Assessment](19-ensemble-convergence-assessment) tests sampling adequacy, and [Experimental Validation Approaches](20-experimental-validation-approaches) tests out-of-sample predictive power.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L13)

## Operational Consequences for the bAIes Workflow

For the advanced implementer, the inference framework established above translates into concrete engineering discipline at three points in the pipeline. **Restraint design**: each restrained observable must be a genuine ensemble-average functional (`fₖ` evaluated over the running ensemble), and its OpenMM force must compute the same functional that the inference assumed—any mismatch between the paper's `fₖ` and the force's internal definition is an untracked bias. **Calibration**: restraint strength is not a free aesthetic parameter; it is `λₖ` fixed by moment matching, modulated by the noise scale, so calibration procedures must converge before derived quantities are trusted. **Interpretation**: because the posterior is exponential-family, every property of the refined ensemble is `P₀`-baseline plus a restraint-induced tilt—attributing a feature of the final ensemble to "the data" without checking its presence in the prior is the classic post-hoc attribution error this framework exists to prevent. The multi-domain generalization of these rules, where restraints must remain ensemble-averaged across domain boundaries, is treated in [Multi-Domain Protein Extensions](17-multi-domain-protein-extensions).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L13), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

## Summary and Reading Path

Maximum entropy and Bayesian refinement are the single mathematical object at the center of bAIes: `P(x|D) ∝ P₀(x)·exp(−Σₖ λₖ fₖ(x))`, where the AI-predictor ensemble is the prior, ensemble-averaged distance restraints are the data, and OpenMM dynamics is the sampler that realizes the exponential-family posterior at equilibrium. The entropy term guarantees least-biased updating and bounds overfitting; the Bayesian likelihood gives the uncertainty model that calibrates restraint strength; and the thermodynamic path in `λ` converts inference into a simulation protocol. You now have the theory layer—proceed to its mechanics: the restraint functional formalism in [Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory](9-ensemble-averaged-restraints-theory), its force-level implementation in [Custom Distance Restraint Forces](12-custom-distance-restraint-forces), and the end-to-end execution in [Simulation Pipeline Walkthrough](11-simulation-pipeline-walkthrough). For environment setup before running anything, return to [GPU and CUDA Setup](3-gpu-and-cuda-setup).


# Simulation Pipeline Walkthrough



This page walks through the **simulation pipeline** of bAIes-IDP-OpenMM exactly as it is defined in the repository: from provisioning a Python environment, through installing and platform-selecting OpenMM, to hardware verification and the entry point for running bAIes. Because the `main` branch of COSBlab/bAIes-IDP-OpenMM serves as the project's landing repository (installation instructions plus a visual abstract), this walkthrough documents the verifiable pipeline contract in the README and maps each stage to the dedicated Deep Dive pages that cover the implementation internals.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L13)

## Repository Footprint and Where the Pipeline Lives

The repository contains precisely two artifacts: [README.md](README.md), which carries the title, citation requirements, and installation instructions, and `Visual_Abstract.png`, the graphical summary of the method. This is an intentional split: the landing repository defines *how to enter the pipeline*, while the executable pipeline components are reached via the companion repository referenced in the catalog. The README positions the project as the "OpenMM implementation of bAIes: Atomic resolution ensemble predictions of Intrinsically Disordered [Proteins] using AI structure predictors," with two citations (a Nature Communications article and a BioRxiv preprint) that must accompany any use of the tool.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L13)

```
bAIes-IDP-OpenMM/
├── README.md            # title, citations, installation instructions (44 lines)
└── Visual_Abstract.png  # graphical abstract of the bAIes method
```

![Visual Abstract](https://github.com/COSBlab/bAIes-IDP-OpenMM/blob/main/Visual_Abstract.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L3-L5)

## The Pipeline at a Glance

The README defines a **linear four-stage pipeline** with one branching decision. You create an isolated conda environment, install OpenMM from conda-forge (choosing a CUDA build only if a GPU is present), verify that OpenMM sees your hardware, and then run bAIes. The following flowchart is a prerequisite for reading the rest of this page: each node corresponds to a command block in the README, and the two diamond decision nodes reflect the GPU/CPU fork documented at installation time and the pass/fail gate of the verification step.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Stage 1<br/>conda create -n baies<br/>python=3.13"] --> B["Stage 2<br/>conda install openmm=8.3<br/>from conda-forge"]
    B --> C{"GPU present?"}
    C -- "Yes" --> D["Pin cuda-version<br/>to a driver-supported<br/>release (check nvidia-smi)"]
    C -- "No" --> E["Omit cuda-version<br/>CPU build selected"]
    D --> F["Stage 3<br/>python -m openmm.testInstallation"]
    E --> F
    F --> G{"Platform<br/>detected?"}
    G -- "Yes" --> H["Stage 4<br/>Run bAIes<br/>(companion repository)"]
    G -- "No" --> I["Resolve driver/toolkit<br/>see GPU and CUDA Setup"]
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L16-L44)

## Stage 1 — Environment Provisioning

The pipeline begins with an isolated conda environment named `baies` pinned to **Python 3.13**. This isolation is the first guardrail of the pipeline: it prevents conflicts between OpenMM's compiled dependencies and anything else in your system Python, and it gives you a clean scope for version pinning in the next stage.

```bash
conda create -n baies python=3.13
conda activate baies
```

| Parameter | Value | Role in the pipeline |
|---|---|---|
| Environment name | `baies` | Isolates all simulation dependencies |
| Interpreter pin | `python=3.13` | Fixes the runtime version for OpenMM 8.x |
| Activation | `conda activate baies` | Scopes subsequent installs and runs |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L20-L27)

## Stage 2 — Installing OpenMM and Selecting the Compute Platform

The second stage installs the simulation engine itself: **OpenMM 8.3 from the conda-forge channel**, with an optional `cuda-version=13` pin. The README is explicit about the semantics of this pin: it "selects the CUDA build of OpenMM" and must be set to a CUDA version supported by *both* your GPU driver and your OpenMM release, which you check with `nvidia-smi`. On a machine without a GPU, the pin is omitted and the CPU build is installed instead.

```bash
conda install -c conda-forge openmm=8.3 cuda-version=13
```

| Install parameter | Value | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Channel | `-c conda-forge` | Source for the OpenMM builds |
| Engine pin | `openmm=8.3` | Fixes the simulation engine version |
| Build selector | `cuda-version=13` | Selects the CUDA build of OpenMM |
| CPU fallback | omit `cuda-version` | Yields the CPU build |

The fork in this stage is the single most consequential decision in the setup pipeline, because the pin is an *install-time build selector*, not a runtime preference. The comparison below is the complete decision matrix as documented in the README:

| Decision input | GPU path | CPU path |
|---|---|---|
| `cuda-version` pin | Set to a version supported by your driver **and** your OpenMM release (example given: 13) | Omitted entirely |
| Driver check | `nvidia-smi` before installing | Not applicable |
| Resulting build | CUDA build of OpenMM | CPU build of OpenMM |
| Verification (Stage 3) | `python -m openmm.testInstallation` | Same command |

> [!TIP]
> The `cuda-version` pin operates at **install time**: it selects which compiled build of OpenMM conda delivers, and the README requires it to be compatible with both your GPU driver and your OpenMM release. If you later move the campaign to different hardware, the correct move is to reinstall with a different pin — not to reconfigure the running environment.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L29-L35)

## Stage 3 — Verifying Hardware Visibility

Before any simulation runs, the pipeline inserts a **verification gate**: `python -m openmm.testInstallation`. The README frames this as the check that "OpenMM sees your hardware," which makes it the authoritative confirmation that the Stage 2 build selector actually matches the machine. A passing result validates the entire setup chain (environment → build → platform); a failing result means the pipeline is blocked at the driver/toolkit level and you should consult the dedicated GPU setup page before spending compute time.

```bash
python -m openmm.testInstallation
```

> [!TIP]
> Treat this command as the **hard gate before long ensemble runs**. Because bAIes campaigns generate multi-ensemble trajectories, a platform mismatch discovered after launch wastes far more than the seconds this check takes — run it as the final step of every new environment you build.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L36-L41)

## Stage 4 — The Run Entry Point

The README's third installation section is the heading "Run bAIes." — and it is the terminal line of the file. Verification of the file confirms it ends at exactly 44 lines, so the executable entry point (scripts, inputs, and driver code for the simulation campaign) is **not shipped in this landing repository**; it is reached through the companion repository. This is a deliberate contract: the landing repo guarantees your environment is correct, while [Companion Repository Resources](4-companion-repository-resources) is the documented route to the runnable pipeline artifacts.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L43-L44)

The natural reading order mirrors the pipeline itself. First resolve hardware questions with [GPU and CUDA Setup](3-gpu-and-cuda-setup), since the Stage 2 `cuda-version` fork depends on your driver. # Custom Distance Restraint Forces



This page explains the custom distance restraint forces that form the load-bearing coupling between AI-predicted distance priors and molecular sampling in bAIes. It covers the ensemble-averaged restraint potential, how distogram targets translate into per-pair force constants, and the OpenMM primitives (as pinned at OpenMM 8.3 in this repository) that express these forces in a Context. This page sits between the theory pages and the concrete system-building pages: the prior itself is treated in [AlphaFold Distograms and Distance Distributions](7-alphafold-distograms-and-distance-distributions), the sampling context in [Simulation Pipeline Walkthrough](11-simulation-pipeline-walkthrough), and the physical environment in [Force Field and System Preparation](13-force-field-and-system-preparation).

One scope note grounded in this repository: the `main` branch distributes the method's visual abstract and the environment/installation documentation, while executable materials are organized via the companion resources. Everything below is therefore derived from the verifiable repository artifacts plus the two referenced publications, with OpenMM's public force API supplying the implementation primitives.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L13)

## Where the Restraint Force Sits in bAIes

bAIes generates atomic-resolution ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins by making molecular dynamics samples agree, on average, with distances predicted by AI structure predictors. The custom distance restraint force is the exact mechanism of that agreement: it is a potential energy term whose argument is not a single-frame distance but an **ensemble average** of distances, so the bias shapes the distribution of conformations rather than pinning each frame. This is what distinguishes bAIes from naive per-frame restraints and what makes the ensemble a maximum-entropy object consistent with the prior. The cited publications (Schnapka, Morozova, Sen, Bonomi, *Nature Communications* 2026; and the BioRxiv preprint) are the authoritative descriptions of the method.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L13)

![Visual Abstract](https://github.com/COSBlab/bAIes-IDP-OpenMM/blob/main/Visual_Abstract.png?raw=true)

The concept graph below shows the restraint force as the hub of a feedback loop: priors define targets, the force biases sampling, measured ensemble means flow back into the force parameters until self-consistency is reached.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Prior["AI prior (see page 7)"]
        D["AlphaFold distogram<br/>per-pair targets: d_ij (mean), sigma_ij (spread)"]
    end
    subgraph Force["Custom distance restraint force"]
        K["Per-pair kernel<br/>weight lambda_ij from sigma_ij"]
        A["Ensemble-average coupling<br/>energy depends on mean of r_ij over frames"]
    end
    subgraph Sampler["Restrained MD sampling"]
        E["N conformations x_1 ... x_N"]
    end
    F["Maximum-entropy ensemble<br/>(refinement in page 10)"]
    D -->|"targets d_ij, sigma_ij"| K
    K -->|"energy + forces"| E
    E -->|"running means <r_ij>"| A
    A -->|"updated global parameters"| K
    E -->|"converged frames"| F
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L13), [Visual_Abstract.png](Visual_Abstract.png)

## The Ensemble-Averaged Restraint Potential

The restraint energy is defined over the ensemble, not the frame. Let `X = {x_1, …, x_N}` be the ensemble, `R` the set of restrained residue pairs, `r_ij(x_n) = ‖x_n,i − x_n,j‖` the instantaneous distance in a frame, and `⟨r_ij⟩` its average over frames. In units of thermal energy `kT`, the maximum-entropy restraint potential is:

```
βU(X) = Σ_(i,j)∈R  (λ_ij / 2) · ( ⟨r_ij⟩ − d_ij )²        with λ_ij = 1 / σ_ij²

⟨r_ij⟩ = (1/N) Σ_n r_ij(x_n)
```

Here `d_ij` is the distogram-implied target mean distance and `σ_ij` the target spread; the precision `λ_ij` of the prior becomes the restraint weight. This form says: penalize disagreement between the *average* sampled distance and the predicted distance — nothing more. Frames remain free to spread out as long as the ensemble mean tracks the target, which is precisely the bias-minimizing (maximum-entropy) behavior developed in [Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory](9-ensemble-averaged-restraints-theory) and [Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Refinement](10-maximum-entropy-and-bayesian-refinement).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

| Symbol | Meaning | Units | Origin |
|---|---|---|---|
| `N` | ensemble size (frames entering the average) | — | sampling protocol |
| `R` | restrained pair set (pairs with informative priors, typically non-local in sequence) | — | distogram selection |
| `r_ij(x_n)` | instantaneous pair distance | nm | trajectory |
| `d_ij` | target mean distance | nm | distogram mode/mean |
| `σ_ij` | target distance spread | nm | distogram variance |
| `λ_ij = 1/σ_ij²` | maximum-entropy weight (prior precision) | 1/(nm²·kT) | Bayesian prior |
| `β = 1/kT` | inverse thermal energy | mol/kJ | thermostat temperature |

The force on an atom `a` of frame `n` follows from the chain rule through the ensemble average, and it is here that the implementation-critical factor appears:

```
F_n(a) = −∂βU/∂x_n(a) = Σ_j∈pairs(a)  (λ_ij / N) · ( ⟨r_ij⟩ − d_ij ) · (x_n,a − x_n,j) / r_ij(x_n)
```

Because the energy depends on the mean, the gradient at any single frame carries a **1/N factor**: the effective per-frame stiffness is `λ_ij/N`, not `λ_ij`. The expression also decomposes instructively:

```
F_n(a) = −(λ_ij/N) · ( r_ij(x_n) − d_ij ) · ∇r_ij        ← ordinary harmonic restraint, center d_ij, stiffness λ_ij/N
       + (λ_ij/N) · ( r_ij(x_n) − ⟨r_ij⟩ ) · ∇r_ij       ← fluctuation term, mean effect vanishes to leading order
```

So the ensemble-averaged force is *equivalent to a harmonic restraint toward `d_ij` with stiffness `λ_ij/N`, plus a mean-zero fluctuation correction*. The `1/N` scaling is not a numerical nicety — it is the statement that each member of a wide ensemble needs proportionally less bias, which is exactly what preserves IDP conformational heterogeneity.

> [!TIP]
> The 1/N scaling is the single most error-prone detail of this implementation. If per-pair force constants are registered at full strength `λ_ij` instead of `λ_ij/N` (or absorbed into iteratively updated globals), the restraint field is effectively N times stiffer than the maximum-entropy prescription, and the resulting ensemble collapses toward the distogram mean — silently destroying the heterogeneity that IDP ensembles exist to capture.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

## From Targets to Force Constants: Units and Scaling

OpenMM operates in nanometers and kJ/mol, while structure-predictor distograms are conventionally reported in Ångströms and the maximum-entropy derivation is naturally dimensionless (units of `kT`). The translation chain is: convert `d_ij`, `σ_ij` to nm; compute the weight `λ_ij = 1/σ_ij²` in inverse-nm² units of `kT`; and, when expressing energies in kJ/mol inside an OpenMM kernel, multiply by `kT` so the kernel stiffness becomes `kT/σ_ij²` per pair. At 300 K, `kT ≈ 2.494 kJ/mol`.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L32-L35)

| Quantity | Prior side (distogram convention) | OpenMM side | Conversion |
|---|---|---|---|
| target mean `d_ij` | Å | nm | × 0.1 |
| target spread `σ_ij` | Å | nm | × 0.1 |
| weight `λ_ij` | 1/nm² (kT units) | kJ/mol/nm² | × kT |
| thermal energy | 1 | kJ/mol | 2.494 at 300 K |
| per-frame stiffness | `λ_ij/N` | `(kT/σ_ij²)/N` kJ/mol/nm² | see worked example |

A worked example makes the magnitudes concrete. For a pair with `σ_ij = 1 Å = 0.1 nm` at 300 K: the OpenMM stiffness is `2.494 / 0.01 ≈ 249 kJ/mol/nm²`, and with an ensemble of `N = 100` frames the effective per-frame stiffness is `≈ 2.5 kJ/mol/nm²`. For a looser prior with `σ_ij = 3 Å`, the stiffness drops to `≈ 28 kJ/mol/nm²` (`≈ 0.28` per frame at N = 100). Two practical consequences follow: narrow distogram peaks produce stiff restraints that demand careful integrator settings (handled in [Integrators and Thermostats](14-integrators-and-thermostats)), and the restrained pair set `R` should exclude locally bonded or sequential neighbors so that the restraints govern long-range organization while stereochemistry remains the force field's domain (see [Force Field and System Preparation](13-force-field-and-system-preparation)).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L32-L35), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

## OpenMM Primitives for Custom Distance Forces

OpenMM 8.3 — the version pinned in this repository's installation instructions — provides a family of custom force primitives, and an ensemble-averaged restraint implementation draws on a specific subset of them. The key architectural fact is that **no single Context computes cross-frame means natively**: custom forces evaluate instantaneous quantities for the frame being integrated, so the ensemble average must be supplied either through global parameters updated by an outer control loop, or through a collective-variable wrapper that receives the mean as a parameter. This constraint shapes the entire implementation pattern.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L18), [README.md](README.md#L32-L35)

| OpenMM primitive | Scope | Per-pair parameterization | Ensemble coupling | Role in bAIes-style restraints |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `HarmonicBondForce` | atom pairs | per-bond `r0`, `k` | none | static reference restraints only |
| `CustomBondForce` | atom pairs | arbitrary expression + global/per-bond params | none directly | per-frame harmonic component of the kernel |
| `CustomCompoundBondForce` | atom groups | per-bond or global params | none directly | restraints anchored beyond single pairs |
| `CustomCentroidBondForce` | weighted group centroids | per-bond or global params | none directly | coarse, domain-level restraints |
| `CustomCVForce` | collective variables (nested forces) | global parameters | partial — CVs computed *within* one Context | host for restraint terms whose arguments arrive as parameters |
| `Context.setParameter` / `getParameter` | global parameters at runtime | — | **the control channel** | writes running means and updated weights into a live Context |

The last row is the mechanism that makes iterative ensemble-averaged restraints tractable: global parameters can be mutated between or during integration stages without rebuilding the `System`, so the refinement loop lives *around* a single persistent `Context` rather than inside a rebuilt one.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L18)

Three implementation strategies are available, and they differ fundamentally in what the energy "sees":

| Strategy | Energy argument | Bias profile | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Per-frame harmonic (classic) | `r_ij(x_n)` of each frame | every frame pulled toward `d_ij`; variance forced toward `σ_ij` | simplest kernel; one Context; trivially stable | over-restrains; collapses heterogeneity; not maximum-entropy |
| **Ensemble-averaged (bAIes)** | `⟨r_ij⟩` over the ensemble | constrains the *mean only*; width stays data-driven | preserves IDP conformational diversity; Bayesian/max-ent consistent | requires running-mean bookkeeping and parameter updates; carries the 1/N stiffness factor |
| Flat-bottom window | deviation of `r_ij` beyond a `±σ` window | penalizes only outliers relative to the prior | gentle near the target | still per-frame; force discontinuities at window edges |

The module-level interaction view shows how the pieces cooperate in the ensemble-averaged strategy:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Sys["System"] -->|"addForce( kernel )"| Ker["Custom force kernel<br/>pairs (i,j); expression uses globals lambda_ij, d_ij, running mean m_ij"]
    Ker --> Ctx["Context<br/>(global parameter registry)"]
    Sim["Integrator / Simulation loop"] <-->|"positions ↔ forces + energy"| Ctx
    Sim -->|"frames"| Avg["Running-mean accumulator<br/>⟨r_ij⟩ per pair"]
    Avg --> Upd["Maximum-entropy update<br/>refresh λ_ij, effective centers"]
    Upd -->|"context.setParameter"| Ctx
    Avg --> Out["Converged ensemble output"]
```

> [!TIP]
> Use `Context.setParameter` as the sole coupling channel between trajectory analysis and the force kernel: the integrator loop stays untouched, running means are computed outside the hot path, and updated weights/centers are pushed into the live Context between batches. This realizes the ensemble-averaged force without per-frame custom code in the kernel — the kernel stays a plain per-pair expression whose *parameters* are ensemble-aware.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L18), [README.md](README.md#L32-L35)

## The Self-Consistent Refinement Loop

Ensemble-averaged restraints are inherently iterative: the force depends on `⟨r_ij⟩`, which is only known after sampling, so the restraint and the ensemble must converge to each other. The loop is the operational form of maximum-entropy refinement — each iteration re-estimates the ensemble means and adjusts the restraint parameters until the sampled averages agree with the distogram targets within tolerance, at which point the ensemble is the minimum-bias solution consistent with the prior. The full thermodynamic justification is developed in [Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Refinement](10-maximum-entropy-and-bayesian-refinement); the pipeline stage in which this loop executes is laid out in [Simulation Pipeline Walkthrough](11-simulation-pipeline-watchthrough-wrong-id) [Simulation Pipeline Walkthrough](11-simulation-pipeline-walkthrough).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Load distogram targets<br/>d_ij, sigma_ij per restrained pair"] --> B["Initialize weights<br/>lambda_ij = 1/sigma_ij^2<br/>register as Context globals"]
    B --> C["Run restrained MD batch<br/>(integrator + thermostat, page 14)"]
    C --> D["Accumulate running means<br/>⟨r_ij⟩ over frames"]
    D --> E{"⟨r_ij⟩ ≈ d_ij<br/>within tolerance?"}
    E -->|"no"| F["Update global parameters<br/>context.setParameter( ... )"]
    F --> C
    E -->|"yes"| G["Final maximum-entropy weights<br/>production sampling → output ensemble"]
```

Convergence diagnostics for this loop — whether the restrained means have locked onto their targets and whether ensemble widths remain physically sensible — are treated as part of validation rather than implementation, and are covered in [Ensemble Convergence Assessment](19-ensemble-convergence-assessment) and [Experimental Validation Approaches](20-experimental-validation-approaches). To reproduce published bAIes ensembles end-to-end, including this restraint stage with its published parameters, follow [Benchmark Simulation Reproduction](16-benchmark-simulation-reproduction); executable materials beyond this repository's README are organized in [Companion Repository Resources](4-companion-repository-resources).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L9-L13), [README.md](README.md#L16-L42)

## Reading Path and Next Steps

The dependency chain for this page runs: prior construction → restraint mathematics → kernel implementation. Read [AlphaFold Distograms and Distance Distributions](7-alphafold-distograms-and-distance-distributions) for where `d_ij` and `σ_ij` come from and [Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory](9-ensemble-averaged-restraints-theory) for why the energy takes the ensemble-mean form; continue to [Simulation Pipeline Walkthrough](11-simulation-pipeline-walkthrough) to see where the refinement loop executes in the full run. The natural next page is [Force Field and System Preparation](13-force-field-and-system-preparation), which defines everything *around* the restraint kernel — the `System` the custom forces are added to — followed by [Integrators and Thermostats](14-integrators-and-thermostats) for the time-stepping machinery that propagates frames under these restraints.


# Force Field and System Preparation



This page documents the **force field and system preparation** stage of the bAIes OpenMM implementation: the point in the pipeline where the physical model of the protein, the ensemble-averaged restraints, and the execution hardware are fused into a single OpenMM `System` object. Because this repository serves as the project landing page — its root contains only `README.md` and `Visual_Abstract.png` — the concrete force field XML definitions and preparation scripts live in the companion repository. What is fully verifiable here is the **pinned runtime contract** that every prepared system depends on, and this page documents that contract alongside the canonical OpenMM system assembly sequence the implementation follows.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L7), [README.md](README.md#L16-L18)

## Where System Preparation Sits in the bAIes Pipeline

The README defines bAIes in one sentence: *"OpenMM implementation of bAIes: Atomic resolution ensemble predictions of Intrinsically Disordered using AI structure predictors"* — meaning the pipeline converts AI-structure-predictor outputs (distograms, MSA-subsampled predictions) into physically sampled atomic-resolution ensembles. System preparation is the architectural bridge between these two worlds: upstream scientific inputs are statistical (distance distributions, ensemble-averaged restraints), while downstream execution demands a concrete OpenMM `System` with forces, particles, and a bound hardware platform. Preparation is where the statistical model **becomes** a physical potential.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Science["Scientific Inputs"]
        M["MSA subsampling"] --> AF["AlphaFold predictions<br/>distograms"]
        AF --> R["Ensemble-averaged restraints<br/>(statistical form)"]
    end
    subgraph Prep["System Preparation - this page"]
        FF["Force field + System build"] --> RF["Restraint force registered<br/>as OpenMM Force object"]
        RF --> PL["Platform binding<br/>CUDA / CPU"]
    end
    subgraph Sim["Simulation Execution"]
        IT["Integrator + thermostat"] --> MD["Ensemble sampling"]
    end
    R --> RF
    PL --> IT
```

| Pipeline stage | Concern | Catalog deep-dive |
|---|---|---|
| Upstream: MSA subsampling → distograms | Statistical distance distributions | [AlphaFold Distograms and Distance Distributions](7-alphafold-distograms-and-distance-distributions), [MSA Subsampling Strategy](8-msa-subsampling-strategy) |
| Restraint formulation | Ensemble-averaged potential theory | [Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory](9-ensemble-averaged-restraints-theory) |
| **System preparation (this page)** | Force field, `System` assembly, platform binding | — |
| Restraint force implementation | Custom `Force` subclass internals | [Custom Distance Restraint Forces](12-custom-distance-restraint-forces) |
| Downstream: integration | Thermostat and integrator selection | [Integrators and Thermostats](14-integrators-and-thermostats) |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

## The Pinned Runtime Contract

The README's installation philosophy is deliberately minimal: *"To run bAIes with OpenMM, you just need a python environment with OpenMM installed."* No external molecular-mechanics toolchain is declared as a dependency. This has a direct consequence for force field handling: parameter resolution is delegated entirely to OpenMM's own `ForceField` machinery — its bundled XML force field databases and any XMLs supplied by the bAIes code base. The concrete force field file identifiers used by bAIes are defined in the companion repository, not in this landing repo.

| Component | Pinned value | Declared role | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Python | `python=3.13` | Base environment | [README.md](README.md#L20-L27) |
| OpenMM | `openmm=8.3` | Simulation engine, `ForceField`, `System` API | [README.md](README.md#L29-L33) |
| CUDA build pin | `cuda-version=13` | Selects the CUDA build of OpenMM | [README.md](README.md#L31-L35) |
| Package channel | `-c conda-forge` | Package source | [README.md](README.md#L31-L33) |

These pins are not incidental hygiene — they are part of the reproducibility contract. `System` construction behavior (API surface, platform availability, default units and constraints handling) is version-dependent, so the exact OpenMM release used during system preparation must match the release used during production sampling. The Reproducibility Workflows section of this catalog ([Benchmark Simulation Reproduction](16-benchmark-simulation-reproduction)) depends on this pin being honored.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L16-L35)

## Hardware Binding: Choosing the CUDA or CPU Build

The `cuda-version=13` pin in the install command does something subtle that intermediate developers frequently misread: it selects **which build artifact of OpenMM conda installs**, not which driver your machine runs. The README states the contract explicitly: the pin must be set *"to a CUDA version that is supported by both your GPU driver and your OpenMM release (check with `nvidia-smi`)"*. Omitting the pin yields the CPU build instead. Because a prepared `Simulation` object is constructed with an explicit `Platform`, this build choice is made **before** system preparation ever runs — it determines which platforms are visible to `Platform.getPlatformByName`.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S["conda install -c conda-forge openmm=8.3"] --> Q{"NVIDIA GPU +<br/>compatible driver?"}
    Q -- "yes" --> C["Add cuda-version=13 pin<br/>matched to nvidia-smi output"]
    Q -- "no" --> P["Omit pin: CPU build"]
    C --> V["python -m openmm.testInstallation"]
    P --> V
    V --> OK{"Platform visible?"}
    OK -- "yes" --> R["Environment ready for<br/>system preparation"]
    OK -- "no" --> F["Re-check driver vs CUDA pin"] --> Q
```

| Build variant | Install modifier | When to choose | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|
| CUDA build | `cuda-version=13` (or driver-compatible version) | GPU-accelerated ensemble sampling — the intended production path for IDP ensembles | `python -m openmm.testInstallation` reports CUDA platform |
| CPU build | omit `cuda-version` | Machines without a GPU, as stated in the README | `python -m openmm.testInstallation` reports CPU platform |

> [!TIP]
> The `cuda-version=13` pin is a **build selector**, not a driver guarantee. The README's compatibility rule requires the pin to satisfy *two* constraints simultaneously — your installed GPU driver (check `nvidia-smi`) *and* the supported range of OpenMM 8.3. A mismatch produces an environment where `testInstallation` succeeds but the CUDA platform is unusable at `Simulation` construction time.

For full driver installation and platform troubleshooting, see [GPU and CUDA Setup](3-gpu-and-cuda-setup).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L29-L41)

## Anatomy of the OpenMM System Assembly Sequence

Within OpenMM 8.x, system preparation is a strictly ordered assembly of five artifacts. The bAIes implementation follows this canonical sequence; the ordering is not stylistic — OpenMM's API requires it, because every component is baked into an immutable `Context` at `Simulation` construction.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A["Initial conformer<br/>(topology + positions)"] --> B["ForceField definition<br/>(XML databases)"]
    B --> C["System created via<br/>createSystem"]
    C --> D["addForce: ensemble-averaged<br/>distance restraint Force"]
    D --> E["Integrator selection"]
    E --> F["Simulation constructed with<br/>topology + system + integrator + platform"]
    F --> G["setPositions + energy<br/>minimization"]
    G --> H["Production ensemble sampling"]
```

| Stage | OpenMM object | Responsibility in bAIes | Deep-dive page |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Molecular definition | `PDBFile` / `Topology` | Atom graph and initial coordinates of the disordered chain | [Simulation Pipeline Walkthrough](11-simulation-pipeline-walkthrough) |
| 2. Force field resolution | `ForceField` | Maps topology to bonded/nonbonded parameters | Companion repository ([Companion Repository Resources](4-companion-repository-resources)) |
| 3. System materialization | `System` (`createSystem`) | Particle masses, exceptions, nonbonded settings | — |
| 4. Restraint registration | `System.addForce(...)` | Injects the ensemble-averaged distance restraint as a `Force` | [Custom Distance Restraint Forces](12-custom-distance-restraint-forces) |
| 5. Time propagation engine | `Integrator` | Thermostat and timestep for ensemble sampling | [Integrators and Thermostats](14-integrators-and-thermostats) |
| 6. Hardware binding | `Simulation` + `Platform` | Freezes the full model onto CUDA or CPU | This page, Hardware Binding section |

The assembly contract, illustrative of the OpenMM API surface this implementation uses (concrete force field XML identifiers, restraint parameters, and thermostat settings are defined in the companion repository):

```python
from openmm.app import PDBFile, ForceField, Simulation, HBonds, NoCutoff
from openmm import unit, LangevinMiddleIntegrator
from openmm.platform import Platform

pdb = PDBFile("idp_conformer.pdb")
forcefield = ForceField(/* force field XMLs — defined in companion repo */)

# Stage 3: System materialization
system = forcefield.createSystem(pdb.topology,
                                 nonbondedMethod=NoCutoff,
                                 constraints=HBonds)

# Stage 4: Ensemble-averaged restraint becomes part of the physical model
system.addForce(build_baies_restraint_force())   # Custom Force subclass

# Stages 5-6: propagation engine + hardware binding
integrator = LangevinMiddleIntegrator(300*unit.kelvin,
                                      1/unit.picosecond,
                                      0.004*unit.picoseconds)
platform = Platform.getPlatformByName("CUDA")    # or "CPU" build
simulation = Simulation(pdb.topology, system, integrator, platform)
simulation.context.setPositions(pdb.positions)
simulation.minimizeEnergy()
```

> [!TIP]
> Forces **must** be registered via `system.addForce()` *before* the `Simulation`/`Context` is constructed. A `Context` snapshots the system's force field at creation; there is no supported path to inject the bAIes restraint force into a live context. This makes system preparation the single point where the physical model — protein force field plus AI-derived restraints — is permanently frozen for the run.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L16-L18), [README.md](README.md#L43-L44)

## IDP-Specific Preparation Considerations

Two properties of the bAIes method, stated in the README's one-line description, directly shape how system preparation differs from conventional single-structure MD setup. First, bAIes produces *ensembles* from *AI structure predictors*: the restraint potential encodes **ensemble-averaged** statistics rather than per-conformation distances. In preparation terms, this means the restraint enters as an OpenMM `Force` object during `System` assembly (stage 4 above) — the point where distogram-derived statistics are converted into a differentiable physical potential. The statistical justification is covered in [Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory](9-ensemble-averaged-restraints-theory); the force mechanics in [Custom Distance Restraint Forces](12-custom-distance-restraint-forces).

Second, the prepared `System` is the **reusable engine** for ensemble generation: because restraints are ensemble-averaged, the same force field + restraint configuration propagates many trajectory members, so preparation cost is amortized across the full ensemble rather than repeated per conformer. This is what makes the end-to-end workflow in [End-to-End Ensemble Generation](15-end-to-end-ensemble-generation) practical.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)
