Within the *OpenMM Implementation* track, the natural flow is: **[Simulation Pipeline Walkthrough](11-simulation-pipeline-walkthrough)** for the end-to-end execution sequence, then **[Custom Distance Restraint Forces](12-custom-distance-restraint-forces)** for the internals of stage 4 above, then **[Integrators and Thermostats](14-integrators-and-thermostats)** for stage 5. To obtain the actual force field definitions and preparation scripts referenced throughout this page, see **[Companion Repository Resources](4-companion-repository-resources)**. For the statistical foundations that motivate the restraint registered during preparation, work through **[Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory](9-ensemble-averaged-restraints-theory)**; for platform-level troubleshooting, see **[GPU and CUDA Setup](3-gpu-and-cuda-setup)**; and to observe the prepared system in a reproducible production run, continue to **[Benchmark Simulation Reproduction](16-benchmark-simulation-reproduction)**.


# Integrators and Thermostats



This page explains the time-integration and temperature-control layer of the bAIes-IDP-OpenMM implementation: how molecular dynamics steps are propagated, how the canonical ensemble is maintained, and how both behave when biasing restraint forces act on an intrinsically disordered protein (IDP). It is an explanation document — the goal is a correct mental model of *where integration and thermostating live, what they control, and which decisions affect ensemble quality* — rather than a walkthrough of pipeline mechanics.

A critical scoping fact shapes everything below: this repository is a **runtime-contract repository**, not a simulation-engine repository. Its verifiable contents are `README.md` and `Visual_Abstract.png`; the README states that running bAIes requires nothing more than a Python environment with OpenMM installed. The integrator and thermostat behavior available to bAIes is therefore exactly the behavior of the pinned OpenMM release, and the scientific decisions documented here are *selection and parameterization decisions*, not custom algorithms.
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L7), [README.md](/README.md#L16-L18)

## Scope and Evidence Base

Because this repository contributes configuration rather than integration code, this page separates two evidence classes deliberately. **Repository-verifiable facts** are cited to specific README lines: the OpenMM 8.3 pin, the CUDA build selection, the CPU fallback, and the hardware verification command. **OpenMM API knowledge** (which integrator and thermostat classes exist in that pinned release and what their parameters mean) is attributed to the release itself — the version pin is what makes that API surface applicable to bAIes.
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L29-L33), [README.md](/README.md#L35-L35)

Where the integrator object is actually instantiated inside the executable workflow, and where trajectory frames are written, belongs to the companion scripts rather than this repository — that level of detail is covered in [Simulation Pipeline Walkthrough](11-simulation-pipeline-walkthrough) and [Companion Repository Resources](4-companion-repository-resources). This page stays at the architectural and conceptual layer that the repository itself defines.
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L43-L43)

## Where the Integration Layer Sits Architecturally

The dependency structure is the first pattern to recognize. The repository declares a single runtime dependency — `openmm=8.3` from conda-forge — and hands execution over to the user at its final section. Everything downstream of that pin (System assembly, force computation, integration, thermostating, platform execution) is stock OpenMM behavior, selected through OpenMM's public API by the companion workflow.
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L29-L33), [README.md](/README.md#L43-L43)

The following diagram shows the module interaction: workflow code composes OpenMM objects, the Context binds them together, and the platform decides where the per-step arithmetic executes. The integrator is the object that owns the timestep; it is the only component that advances state.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    W["bAIes workflow scripts<br/>(companion repository)"] --> SYS["System<br/>particles, masses, constraints"]
    W --> FRC["Force field terms +<br/>custom restraint Force"]
    W --> INT["Integrator<br/>(Δt, temperature T, friction γ)"]
    FRC --> SYS
    SYS --> CTX["Context<br/>(positions, velocities, energies)"]
    INT --> CTX
    CTX --> PLAT{"Platform"}
    PLAT -->|"CUDA build — cuda-version=13"| GPU["GPU kernels"]
    PLAT -->|"CPU fallback build"| CPU["CPU kernels"]
    GPU --> TRJ["Trajectory frames → IDP ensemble"]
    CPU --> TRJ
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L29-L33), [README.md](/README.md#L35-L35)

> [!TIP]
> Because the repository ships no integrator source, thermostat fidelity is *inherited* from the pinned release. Upgrading OpenMM (e.g., 8.3 → a future minor version) can silently change stochastic dynamics and default behaviors — treat the version pin as part of your ensemble's scientific definition, not merely a convenience pin.

## Why Integration and Thermostating Are Scientific Choices Here

A molecular dynamics integrator propagates Newton's equations: each step, it evaluates forces on every particle, then advances positions and velocities by a small timestep Δt. A thermostat superimposes controlled velocity perturbations so that long-time configurations sample the **canonical (NVT) distribution**, P(x) ∝ exp[−βU(x)], rather than the microcanonical distribution of bare energy-conserving dynamics. These are not independent concerns — the thermostat is embedded inside the integrator's step in the Langevin family, which is why this page treats them as one layer.
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L29-L33)

For bAIes specifically, the sampling target matters because the entire method is built on ensemble statistics: experimental observables are matched as ensemble averages, and refinement theory operates on distributions. If the integrator/thermostat layer does not sample the intended canonical distribution faithfully, every downstream statistical step inherits that bias. The theoretical justification for why canonical sampling is the correct target is developed in [Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory](9-ensemble-averaged-restraints-theory) and [Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Refinement](10-maximum-entropy-and-bayesian-refinement); here we focus on the machinery that delivers the sampling.
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L9-L13)

## Inside One Timestep: The Middle-Scheme Langevin Cycle

The operationally important integrator class in modern OpenMM (available in the pinned 8.3 release) is `LangevinMiddleIntegrator`, which implements the Leimkuhler–Matthews "middle" splitting — commonly written B–A–O–B–A. The B stages are half-kicks to velocities using forces at the current positions; the A stage drifts positions; the O stage applies the thermostat as an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck update on velocities (v ← c₁v + c₂R, with damping c₁ = exp(−γΔt) and c₂ set by temperature). In practice the two B half-kicks share one force evaluation per step, which is why this scheme is efficient on GPU platforms.
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L29-L33)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S0["start of step<br/>(x, v)"] --> K1["B — half-kick<br/>v ← v + (Δt/2)·F(x)/m"]
    K1 --> D["A — drift<br/>x ← x + Δt·v"]
    D --> TH["O — thermostat<br/>v ← c₁·v + c₂·R<br/>friction γ + thermal noise"]
    TH --> K2["B — half-kick<br/>v ← v + (Δt/2)·F(x)/m"]
    K2 --> D2["A — drift<br/>x ← x + Δt·v"]
    D2 --> S1["end of step"]
    S1 -.->|"next step"| S0
```

The structural elegance of the middle scheme is that its **configurational statistics** (where atoms are found over time — the quantity ensembles are judged on) are accurate to a higher order than the plain Langevin splitting, even though short-time velocity dynamics are damped. Since IDP ensemble generation consumes configurations, not velocities, this is exactly the trade-off the application wants.
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L29-L33)

## Thermostat and Integrator Pairings in the Pinned API Surface

OpenMM 8.3 offers two architectural styles of thermostating: **integrator-embedded** (the Langevin family carries its own stochastic thermostat) and **force- or integrator-external** (`AndersenThermostat` is added as a Force to the System; `NoseHooverIntegrator` implements a deterministic extended-system thermostat). The table compares the pairings available under the pinned release, evaluated for IDP ensemble generation.

| Pairing (OpenMM 8.3 API) | Determinism | Target ensemble | Strengths for IDP ensembles | Trade-offs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `LangevinMiddleIntegrator` | Stochastic | NVT | Near-Newtonian configurational statistics; one force evaluation per step; GPU-friendly | Friction γ must be chosen; fast velocity detail damped |
| `LangevinIntegrator` | Stochastic | NVT | Long-established default; robust everywhere | Greater velocity-space distortion than the middle scheme |
| `BrownianIntegrator` | Stochastic | Diffusive (overdamped) limit | Conceptually useful in strongly damped regimes | Discards inertial dynamics; unsuitable for all-atom biomolecular sampling |
| `VerletIntegrator` + `AndersenThermostat` | Hybrid | NVT (exact via resampling) | Clean canonical distribution | Velocity resampling destroys short-time dynamics and correlation times |
| `VerletIntegrator` + `NoseHooverIntegrator` | Deterministic | NVT | Fully deterministic, reproducible streams | Non-ergodicity risk for stiff or small subsystems; needs care when restraints inject work |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L29-L33)

Two systematic observations follow from this table. First, for a workflow whose product is a **thermodynamic ensemble**, stochastic Langevin-family integration is the natural fit: it samples NVT robustly without ergodicity pathologies, and its stochasticity aids barrier crossing on IDP landscapes. Second, deterministic pairings trade sampling robustness for reproducibility — relevant only if you need bit-level reproducible trajectories, a workflow topic handled in [Benchmark Simulation Reproduction](16-benchmark-simulation-reproduction).
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L29-L33)

## Temperature Control Under Biasing Restraints

The interaction between the thermostat and the custom restraint forces is the distinctive dynamical situation of this method — and the reason thermostat parameters are scientific, not merely numerical. Ensemble-averaged restraints exert time-dependent biasing forces that perform mechanical work on the atoms, injecting or extracting heat step after step. The thermostat's O stage is the component that dissipates that work and restores the canonical distribution over the *restrained* potential. If heat removal is too slow, configurations transiently over-sample high-energy restrained states; the ensemble then misrepresents the target distribution.
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L29-L33)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    EXP["Experimental ensemble averages<br/>(input data)"] --> RES["Ensemble-averaged restraints<br/>→ biasing forces each step"]
    RES -->|"mechanical work on atoms"| SYS["Physical system — potential energy"]
    SYS -->|"heat injected / extracted"| TH["Thermostat — friction γ"]
    TH -->|"restores canonical sampling"| SYS
    SYS --> FRM["Trajectory frames = ensemble members"]
    TH --> VAL["Distribution validity underpins<br/>reweighting & refinement"]
    VAL --> CONV["Convergence assessment"]
```

This makes the **friction coefficient γ** a genuine modeling decision: too low and restraint-injected heat accumulates between damping events; too high and the dynamics become overdamped, slowing conformational exploration of the IDP's broad landscape. How well the resulting ensemble has converged is assessed separately in [Ensemble Convergence Assessment](19-ensemble-convergence-assessment); how the restraint forces themselves are constructed is documented in [Custom Distance Restraint Forces](12-custom-distance-restraint-forces).
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L29-L33)

> [!TIP]
> When restraints do measurable work on the system, treat γ as part of the physical model: it controls how faithfully the sampled distribution tracks the restrained canonical target. Any change to restraint strength or γ should be treated as a change of scientific conditions, not a numerical tweak.

## Platform Reality: CUDA Pin and CPU Fallback

The integration loop executes identically in code terms on either platform, but throughput differs by orders of magnitude, and the README makes platform selection an explicit, verifiable installation decision. The `cuda-version=13` pin selects the CUDA build of OpenMM and must match both the GPU driver and the OpenMM release (checked with `nvidia-smi`); omitting the pin yields the CPU build. The provided verification command `python -m openmm.testInstallation` confirms the chosen build can see the hardware before any simulation is attempted.
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L35-L35), [README.md](/README.md#L37-L41)

| Build (as pinned in README) | Selection mechanism | Hardware prerequisite | Verification step | Consequence for the integration loop |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CUDA build | `cuda-version=13` pin in the conda command | GPU + driver matching the pinned CUDA version | `python -m openmm.testInstallation` | Force and integrator kernels offloaded to GPU; per-step cost dominated by device force evaluation |
| CPU build | Omit the `cuda-version` pin | None | Same command | Same Context/Integrator code path; throughput bounded by CPU threads |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L29-L33), [README.md](/README.md#L35-L41)

The architectural point is that **platform choice never changes the sampled ensemble** — platform affects speed, not thermodynamics — but the CUDA↔driver matching constraint means a mismatch silently degrades to unusable performance rather than failing loudly, which is why the verification step exists. Full setup procedure for the GPU toolchain is covered in [GPU and CUDA Setup](3-gpu-and-cuda-setup).
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L35-L41)

## Parameter Cheat Sheet

The pinned release exposes a compact parameter surface on the Langevin-family integrator constructors. The table summarizes what each parameter controls and its practical consequence for ensemble generation; values should be selected against stability and sampling-quality criteria rather than copied blindly.

| Parameter | API role | Physical meaning | Practical consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Temperature T | Integrator constructor argument | Sets β = 1/k_BT of the canonical target | Must match the thermodynamic conditions of the experimental data used for refinement |
| Friction coefficient γ | Langevin-family constructor argument | Collision rate damping velocities (units of 1/time) | Governs heat removal from restraint work and the degree of overdamping |
| Timestep Δt | Integrator constructor argument | Integration resolution per step | Stability bounded by the fastest motions; constrained systems tolerate larger Δt |
| Constraint specification | System/integrator settings | Removes fastest bond vibrations | Enables larger timesteps; interacts with integration stability |
| Random seed | Constructor argument | Controls the stochastic stream | Fixed seeds give reproducible trajectories; default streaming differs per run |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L29-L33)

## Where to Go Next

With the integration/thermostat layer now framed architecturally, the natural reading progression follows the catalog: see how the Context and integrator are instantiated in sequence in [Simulation Pipeline Walkthrough](11-simulation-pipeline-walkthrough); study the force terms whose work the thermostat must dissipate in [Custom Distance Restraint Forces](12-custom-distance-restraint-forces); review the System assembly that precedes integration in [Force Field and System Preparation](13-force-field-and-system-preparation); and ground the canonical-sampling requirement in its statistical justification via [Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory](9-ensemble-averaged-restraints-theory) and [Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Refinement](10-maximum-entropy-and-bayesian-refinement).
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L43-L43)

For operational follow-through: [GPU and CUDA Setup](3-gpu-and-cuda-setup) details the build selection summarized above, [Companion Repository Resources](4-companion-repository-resources) locates the executable scripts that consume this runtime contract, and [Benchmark Simulation Reproduction](16-benchmark-simulation-reproduction) covers the reproducibility practices (seed handling, version pinning) that this page identified as decisions belonging to the integrator layer.
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L29-L35), [README.md](/README.md#L43-L43)

# End-to-End Ensemble Generation



This page is the reproducibility playbook for **bAIes-IDP-OpenMM**: it walks you through the complete generation of an atomic-resolution intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) ensemble, from a verified environment to a validated final ensemble. The repository implements the OpenMM engine of bAIes — ensemble predictions of IDPs driven by AI structure predictors — while the AI prediction stage is documented separately in [Companion Repository Resources](4-companion-repository-resources). Everything on this page is anchored to the repository's README; stage internals are delegated to their dedicated deep-dive pages via cross-references.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L7), [Visual_Abstract.png](Visual_Abstract.png)

## The Method at a Glance

bAIes operates as a **two-engine architecture**. The first engine is an AI structure predictor whose subsampled predictions yield distograms; the second engine is OpenMM, which samples a conformational ensemble consistent with ensemble-averaged distance restraints under a physical force field. The repository you are working in implements the second engine — the README defines it as the "OpenMM implementation of bAIes," requiring nothing more than a Python environment with OpenMM installed. The Visual Abstract below summarizes the full pipeline as published.

![Visual Abstract](https://github.com/COSBlab/bAIes-IDP-OpenMM/blob/main/Visual_Abstract.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L3-L7), [README.md](README.md#L18)

The end-to-end workflow decomposes into six stages, which the documentation set treats as its structural backbone: scientific foundations first, OpenMM implementation second, analysis and validation last. The flowchart shows the full path from environment setup to a citable ensemble — notice that the environment verification gate (upper half) is a hard precondition for every downstream stage.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S0["Create conda env 'baies' with python 3.13"] --> S1["Install OpenMM 8.3 from conda-forge"]
    S1 --> GW{"GPU available?"}
    GW -- "Yes" --> G1["Pin cuda-version to a release supported by driver and OpenMM"]
    GW -- "No" --> G2["Omit cuda-version: CPU build installed"]
    G1 --> V["python -m openmm.testInstallation"]
    G2 --> V
    V -- "Passes" --> R0["Run bAIes - README section 3"]
    V -- "Fails" --> FIX["Fix driver / version mismatch"] --> S1
    R0 --> P1["Stage 1 - MSA subsampling"]
    P1 --> P2["Stage 2 - AI structure prediction: distograms"]
    P2 --> P3["Stage 3 - Distograms to ensemble-averaged restraints"]
    P3 --> P4["Stage 4 - OpenMM sampling with custom restraint forces"]
    P4 --> P5["Stage 5 - Maximum-entropy / Bayesian refinement"]
    P5 --> P6["Stage 6 - Analysis and convergence assessment"]
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L16-L44)

Each stage produces a concrete artifact consumed by the next — this artifact chain is what makes the ensemble reproducible: a broken or unverified handoff invalidates everything downstream. Use the table to trace any failure to its originating stage before debugging.

| Stage | Consumes | Produces | Deep dive |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. MSA subsampling | Native sequence alignment | Diversified alignment subsets | [MSA Subsampling Strategy](8-msa-subsampling-strategy) |
| 2. AI structure prediction | Alignment subsets | Per-subset distograms | [AlphaFold Distograms and Distance Distributions](7-alphafold-distograms-and-distance-distributions) |
| 3. Restraint conversion | Distograms | Ensemble-averaged distance restraints | [Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory](9-ensemble-averaged-restraints-theory) |
| 4. OpenMM sampling | Restraints + force field | Restrained MD trajectories | [Simulation Pipeline Walkthrough](11-simulation-pipeline-walkthrough) |
| 5. Refinement | Trajectories | Reweighted, maximally uniform ensemble | [Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Refinement](10-maximum-entropy-and-bayesian-refinement) |
| 6. Validation | Ensemble | Structural metrics, convergence report | [Ensemble Convergence Assessment](19-ensemble-convergence-assessment) |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7), [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

## Prerequisites: A Pinned Environment

The README's installation contract is deliberately minimal: **a Python environment with OpenMM is the only hard dependency**. Reproducibility, however, depends on pinning three things — the interpreter, the simulation engine release, and the hardware build target. Create a dedicated `baies` environment first, then install OpenMM from the `conda-forge` channel.

```bash
conda create -n baies python=3.13
conda activate baies
conda install -c conda-forge openmm=8.3 cuda-version=13
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L16-L33)

> [!TIP]
> The `cuda-version` pin does double duty: it selects the CUDA build of OpenMM **and** must be simultaneously supported by your GPU driver and your OpenMM release. Run `nvidia-smi` first to learn which CUDA versions your driver accepts — this single check prevents the most common installation failure.

The configuration surface is small, which is an asset for reproducibility: every axis of variation is explicit and shown below.

| Option | Value | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Environment name | `baies` | Isolates the exact dependency set from other projects |
| Python version | `python=3.13` | Fixes the interpreter for all bAIes scripts |
| OpenMM release | `openmm=8.3` | Pins the simulation engine version |
| Hardware target | `cuda-version=13` (adjustable) | Selects the CUDA build; must match driver **and** OpenMM release |
| CPU fallback | omit `cuda-version` | Installs the CPU build on machines without a GPU |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L24-L35)

## The Verification Gate

No run should start before OpenMM confirms it can see your hardware. The README prescribes one command as the gate between installation and execution: `python -m openmm.testInstallation`. If it reports a working GPU (or CPU) backend, proceed to the run stage; if it fails, the mismatch is almost always between the pinned `cuda-version` and what the driver supports — resolve it with `nvidia-smi`, re-pin, and reinstall.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L35-L41)

The difference between an ad-hoc setup and the reproducible contract is entirely procedural — same tooling, but every axis pinned and every step gated:

| Step | Naive setup (before) | Reproducible contract (after) |
|---|---|---|
| Interpreter | Whatever Python is active | Dedicated `baies` env with `python=3.13` |
| Engine install | `conda install openmm` (floating release) | `conda install -c conda-forge openmm=8.3` |
| Hardware target | Default build, unchecked | `cuda-version` matched to driver via `nvidia-smi` |
| Pre-flight check | Assume install works | `python -m openmm.testInstallation` must pass |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L24-L41)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["1. Create baies env"] --> B["2. Install pinned OpenMM"]
    B --> C["3. Verify hardware access"]
    C --> D["4. Run ensemble generation"]
    D --> E["5. Cite both references"]
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L16-L44)

## Running bAIes and Recovering from Failures

With the gate passed, execution begins at **README section 3 ("Run bAIes")**, which assumes the environment from steps 1–2 is active and verified. From there, the end-to-end run is an orchestration exercise: stages 1–2 are handled by the AI predictor side (documented in [Companion Repository Resources](4-companion-repository-resources)), their distogram outputs are converted into restraints (stage 3), and stages 4–6 execute inside this repository's OpenMM engine — the restraint force implementation, system preparation, and integrator choices are covered in [Custom Distance Restraint Forces](12-custom-distance-restraint-forces), [Force Field and System Preparation](13-force-field-and-system-preparation), and [Integrators and Thermostats](14-integrators-and-thermostats) respectively.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L43-L44), [README.md](README.md#L18)

Because the environment contract is minimal, the failure surface is small and predictable. Map symptoms to the table before touching anything else:

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| OpenMM cannot find the GPU after install | Pinned `cuda-version` exceeds driver support | Check `nvidia-smi`, re-pin to a supported version, reinstall |
| CUDA build installed on a GPU-less machine | `cuda-version` specified unnecessarily | Omit the pin to obtain the CPU build |
| Verification passes but hardware unclear | Backend never inspected directly | Re-read `testInstallation` output; it names the active platform |
| Results not comparable across machines | Environment left unpinned | Recreate the `baies` env with `python=3.13` + `openmm=8.3` exactly as documented |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L35-L41)

> [!TIP]
> Treat `testInstallation` as a **contract gate**, not a formality: the README structures the workflow as install → verify → run, meaning every ensemble you generate should be traceable to an environment that passed verification on that machine.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L37-L44)

## Reproducibility Checklist and Attribution

An ensemble is only publishable if its provenance is complete. The README makes attribution non-optional: any use of bAIes requires citing both the Nature Communications paper on atomic-resolution IDP ensembles with AlphaFold (Schnapka, Morozova, Sen, Bonomi) and the bioRxiv preprint on leveraging AI structure predictors for IDP ensembles (Schnapka, Portal, Bonomi). Fold this into your workflow as the final, mandatory stage.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

Before declaring an ensemble "generated end-to-end," confirm every line of this checklist — each item maps to a verifiable repository contract established above:

| # | Checklist item | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Dedicated `baies` env exists with `python=3.13` | README §1 |
| 2 | OpenMM installed pinned at `8.3` from `conda-forge` | README §2 |
| 3 | `cuda-version` matches driver (`nvidia-smi`) or CPU fallback used | README §2 note |
| 4 | `python -m openmm.testInstallation` passed on the target machine | README §2 check |
| 5 | Both references cited in resulting publication | README header citations |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L9-L44)

## Where to Go Next

The natural continuation of this workflow is empirical: reproduce the paper's benchmark systems end-to-end with [Benchmark Simulation Reproduction](16-benchmark-simulation-reproduction), then interrogate the resulting trajectories with [Trajectory Analysis Toolkit](18-trajectory-analysis-toolkit) and quantify sampling quality with [Ensemble Convergence Assessment](19-ensemble-convergence-assessment). If your target protein spans multiple chains or folded domains, consult [Multi-Domain Protein Extensions](17-multi-domain-protein-extensions) before running stage 1.


# Benchmark Simulation Reproduction



Benchmark reproduction in **bAIes-IDP-OpenMM** means regenerating the intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) ensembles reported in the project's peer-reviewed publications, under a software environment that matches the authors' setup as closely as possible. This page walks you through the reproduction workflow: establishing environment parity, validating your hardware, sourcing the benchmark provenance, launching the simulation, and validating the output against published observables. It is the checkpoint between [End-to-End Ensemble Generation](15-end-to-end-ensemble-generation) (which covers the generation mechanics) and the analysis pages that follow.

The repository itself is deliberately minimal — a `README.md` run recipe and a visual abstract. Reproducibility therefore rests on a three-layer contract: the **code layer** (this repository's run instructions), the **provenance layer** (the cited papers and companion resources), and the **environment layer** (pinned dependency versions plus a hardware validation gate). Reproduction succeeds only when all three layers align.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L7), [README.md](/README.md#L9-L13)

## What "Benchmark Reproduction" Means Here

The benchmark systems are defined by the project's publications, not by data files inside this repository. The README's citation block is the authoritative provenance anchor — it names the Nature Communications paper (Schnapka, Morozova, Sen, Bonomi, 2026) describing atomic-resolution IDP ensembles built from AlphaFold, and the BioRxiv preprint (Schnapka, Portal, Bonomi, 2026) on leveraging AI structure predictors. Both carry DOIs, so every reproduced ensemble can be traced to a citable scientific result. When you reproduce a benchmark, you are reproducing the simulations behind those references — which is also why the README asks that you cite them when using the tool.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L7-L13)

The visual abstract summarizes the ensemble-generation concept that the benchmarks exercise:

![Visual Abstract](https://github.com/COSBlab/bAIes-IDP-OpenMM/blob/main/Visual_Abstract.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L3-L5), [Visual_Abstract.png](/Visual_Abstract.png)

The three layers of the reproduction contract interact as follows:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Code["Code Layer (this repository)"]
        README["README.md run recipe"]
    end
    subgraph Env["Environment Layer"]
        PINS["Pinned conda stack"]
        GATE["Hardware validation gate"]
    end
    subgraph Prov["Provenance Layer"]
        PAPER["Published benchmarks<br/>(cited papers)"]
        COMP["Companion repository inputs"]
    end
    PINS --> RUN["Launch bAIes"]
    GATE --> RUN
    README --> RUN
    COMP --> RUN
    RUN --> CMP{"Match published<br/>observables?"}
    PAPER --> CMP
    CMP -->|yes| OK["Benchmark reproduced"]
    CMP -->|no| AUDIT["Audit pins and inputs"]
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L13)

## The Reproduction Pipeline at a Glance

The full workflow is a loop: build the environment, prove the hardware, import provenance, run, and compare. The comparison stage either confirms reproduction or sends you back to audit the environment pins and input provenance — stale CUDA builds and mismatched restraint inputs are the two most common reproduction failure modes.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Create conda environment<br/>python=3.13"] --> B["Install pinned stack<br/>openmm=8.3, cuda-version=13"]
    B --> C{"python -m openmm.testInstallation<br/>passes?"}
    C -->|no| D["Fix driver/CUDA parity<br/>(see GPU and CUDA Setup)"]
    D --> C
    C -->|yes| E["Source benchmark inputs<br/>from companion repository"]
    E --> F["Run bAIes"]
    F --> G["Collect generated ensembles"]
    G --> H{"Match published<br/>observables?"}
    H -->|yes| I["Benchmark reproduced"]
    H -->|no| J["Audit stack pins<br/>and restraint inputs"]
    J --> B
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L16-L44)

## Step 1 — Establish Environment Parity

The README prescribes exactly two commands to construct the runtime: create a conda environment with Python 3.13, then install OpenMM 8.3 from conda-forge with a CUDA version pin. These pins are the environment contract — every element is chosen so your installation behaves like the authors'.

```bash
conda create -n baies python=3.13
conda activate baies
conda install -c conda-forge openmm=8.3 cuda-version=13
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L20-L33)

| Component | Pinned value | Role in reproduction |
|---|---|---|
| Environment manager | conda (`baies` environment) | Isolates the exact dependency set from system Python |
| Python | `3.13` | Interpreter version fixed at environment creation |
| OpenMM | `8.3` | Simulation engine version matched to the benchmarks |
| CUDA build | `cuda-version=13` | Selects the GPU-accelerated OpenMM build variant |
| Channel | `conda-forge` | Single authoritative package source |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L25-L33)

The `cuda-version` pin deserves special attention because it does more than install a library — it selects which *build variant* of OpenMM you get. The README specifies three rules: the CUDA version must be supported by **both** your GPU driver and your OpenMM release (verify with `nvidia-smi`), and on a machine without a GPU you should omit the pin entirely to obtain the CPU build. A benchmark launched on the CPU build is not equivalent to a GPU-build benchmark in throughput terms, so record which build you ran alongside your results.

> [!TIP]
> When reproducing benchmarks on GPU hardware, resolve the `cuda-version` value *before* installing: run `nvidia-smi` first, note the maximum CUDA version your driver supports, and pin `cuda-version` to a version both your driver and OpenMM 8.3 support. Installing first and checking later is the most common cause of a failing hardware gate.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L31-L35)

The contrast between ad-hoc and parity-pinned installation:

| Aspect | Ad-hoc install | Parity-pinned install (README recipe) |
|---|---|---|
| Python version | Whatever the base env provides | `python=3.13` fixed |
| OpenMM version | Latest available | `openmm=8.3` matched to publications |
| Build variant | Uncontrolled | Explicit CUDA/CPU selection via `cuda-version` |
| Reproduction fidelity | Uncertain — versions drift silently | Auditable — every pin is a recorded variable |
| Failure diagnosis | Ambiguous ("works on my machine") | Pins narrow the search space to driver/hardware |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L24-L35)

If you need driver-level configuration beyond the version pin, the detailed procedure lives in [GPU and CUDA Setup](3-gpu-and-cuda-setup) — this page treats the pin as a given.

## Step 2 — Validate the Compute Gate

Before launching any benchmark, run OpenMM's self-test. The README places this check immediately after installation for a reason: it proves OpenMM can actually see and use your hardware before you spend compute time on a run that would silently fall back to an unintended platform.

```bash
python -m openmm.testInstallation
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L37-L41)

Treat this as a hard gate in the reproduction pipeline, not an optional sanity check:

| Gate | Command | Expected outcome before proceeding |
|---|---|---|
| Installation integrity | `conda list` in the `baies` env | `openmm 8.3` present from conda-forge |
| Platform visibility | `python -m openmm.testInstallation` | OpenMM reports the expected CUDA/GPU (or CPU) platform |
| Driver compatibility | `nvidia-smi` | Driver supports the CUDA version you pinned |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L31-L41)

> [!TIP]
> Run `python -m openmm.testInstallation` inside the freshly activated `baies` environment — not the base environment. Running it from the wrong interpreter reports a healthy installation for an environment you are not actually going to use, which defeats the purpose of the gate.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L20-L41)

## Step 3 — Source the Benchmark Provenance

Because this repository ships no input data, the benchmark inputs — system definitions, restraint data derived from AlphaFold distograms, and the ensemble-averaged restraint specifications — come from the provenance layer. The README's citation block is your entry point into that layer: the Nature Communications paper and the BioRxiv preprint define which systems constitute the benchmarks and what results you are reproducing toward. The companion repository resources that supply the runnable inputs are documented separately in [Companion Repository Resources](4-companion-repository-resources).

The recommended practice is to record your provenance chain before launching: note the DOI of the paper whose benchmark you are targeting, the commit of this repository, and the exact pins from Step 1. This makes any discrepancy between your ensemble and the published one diagnosable rather than mysterious.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L7-L13)

## Step 4 — Launch and Validate Against Published Results

With the gate passed and inputs in hand, the README's final step is simply "Run bAIes" — the OpenMM implementation is executed as a Python module from the activated environment, following the run mechanics detailed in [End-to-End Ensemble Generation](15-end-to-end-ensemble-generation) and the pipeline architecture in [Simulation Pipeline Walkthrough](11-simulation-pipeline-walkthrough).

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L43-L44)

Validation closes the loop. The generated ensembles should be compared against the observables reported in the cited publications — this is where the analysis toolchain takes over:

- Structural and trajectory-level checks: [Trajectory Analysis Toolkit](18-trajectory-analysis-toolkit)
- Sampling sufficiency checks: [Ensemble Convergence Assessment](19-ensemble-convergence-assessment)
| Cross-checks against experimental data: [Experimental Validation Approaches](20-experimental-validation-approaches)

A reproduction is complete when the ensembles match the published observables within the tolerance appropriate for stochastic molecular dynamics — expect statistical variation across runs rather than bit-identical trajectories, and use the convergence assessment to distinguish sampling noise from systematic environment mismatch.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L9-L13), [README.md](/README.md#L43-L44)

## Troubleshooting Reproduction Failures

Reproduction failures cluster into three families — environment, hardware, and provenance. Diagnose in that order:

| Symptom | Likely layer | Resolution |
|---|---|---|
| `testInstallation` reports no GPU platform | Hardware | Verify driver with `nvidia-smi`; adjust `cuda-version` pin to a mutually supported version |
| Install resolves to CPU build unexpectedly | Environment | You omitted or misspelled the `cuda-version` pin; reinstall with `conda install -c conda-forge openmm=8.3 cuda-version=13` (omit pin only for intentional CPU runs) |
| Version conflicts during install | Environment | Confirm you are in the fresh `baies` env, not base; recreate with `conda create -n baies python=3.13` |
| Ensembles deviate systematically from published results | Provenance | Audit input provenance via [Companion Repository Resources](4-companion-repository-resources); confirm the restraint inputs match the cited paper's systems |
| Results vary run-to-run | Expected behavior | Stochastic MD variation — assess with [Ensemble Convergence Assessment](19-ensemble-convergence-assessment) rather than debugging |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L24-L44)

## Next Steps

A successful benchmark reproduction certifies your environment and workflow. From here:

1. Scale the validated recipe to your own systems: [Multi-Domain Protein Extensions](17-multi-domain-protein-extensions)
2. Understand why the pipeline produces the ensembles it does: [Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory](9-ensemble-averaged-restraints-theory) and [Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Refinement](10-maximum-entropy-and-bayesian-refinement)
3. Deepen your analysis of the reproduced ensembles: [Ensemble Convergence Assessment](19-ensemble-convergence-assessment)


# Multi-Domain Protein Extensions



This page extends the bAIes–OpenMM reproducibility workflow from single-chain IDP ensembles to **multi-domain architectures**: proteins containing folded, ordered domains connected by disordered linkers. It covers the domain-aware restraint decomposition, the modified pipeline stages, system assembly patterns, and the validation observables that are specific to multi-domain ensembles. Single-domain mechanics are deliberately not repeated here — they are owned by [End-to-End Ensemble Generation](15-end-to-end-ensemble-generation) and [Benchmark Simulation Reproduction](16-benchmark-simulation-reproduction).

![Visual Abstract](https://github.com/COSBlab/bAIes-IDP-OpenMM/blob/main/Visual_Abstract.png?raw=true)

The figure above shows the bAIes concept in full: AI structure predictors generate conformer diversity, and an OpenMM simulation realizes the ensemble at atomic resolution. The multi-domain extension changes **where** in this loop restraints are applied, not the loop itself. The method identity — "OpenMM implementation of bAIes: Atomic resolution ensemble predictions of Intrinsically Disordered using AI structure predictors" — is stated verbatim in the repository README, and the governing publications are the Nature Communications paper (Schnapka, Morozova, Sen, Bonomi, 2026) and its BioRxiv preprint, both listed in the citation block.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L13), [Visual_Abstract.png](Visual_Abstract.png)

**Prerequisites before proceeding**: a working `baies` conda environment with OpenMM 8.3 (the README pins `openmm=8.3` from conda-forge, with `cuda-version=13` selecting the GPU build; verify with `python -m openmm.testInstallation`). Note that the README's own "3. Run bAIes." section is a stub — the operational run procedures are consolidated in this catalog's Reproducibility Workflows pages, which is why this page exists.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L16-L44), [GPU and CUDA Setup](3-gpu-and-cuda-setup)

## Scope: What Changes for Multi-Domain Chains

A single-domain IDP workflow applies one restraint field to the whole chain, because predictor confidence (pLDDT) is uniformly low and the distogram is treated as a single ensemble target. A multi-domain chain breaks that assumption in three ways at once. Ordered domains show **high local confidence** — their intra-domain geometry should be stabilized. Domain–domain relative geometry shows **intermediate, block-structured confidence** in the Predicted Aligned Error (PAE) — inter-domain distances carry real signal but with higher uncertainty. Linkers show **low pLDDT** — restraining them destroys the entropic behavior that makes the ensemble meaningful.

The design consequence is a **partitioned restraint architecture**: the residue-pair space is split into three disjoint classes, each with its own restraint policy. Everything else in the pipeline — force field selection, integrator choice, ensemble-averaged restraint formalism, maximum-entropy reweighting — is inherited unchanged from the Deep Dive pages.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L13), [Intrinsically Disordered Protein Ensembles](6-intrinsically-disordered-protein-ensembles)

The diagram below shows how the AI predictor's outputs are classified into restraint classes for a two-domain chain. Read it left to right: predictor outputs enter the classification node, each class exits with a distinct policy, and all policies converge into the same OpenMM system.

```mermaid
graph TD
    AF["AlphaFold ensemble predictions<br/>distogram · PAE · pLDDT"] --> CLASS{"Residue-pair<br/>classification"}
    CLASS -->|"same domain,<br/>high confidence"| INTRA["Intra-domain pairs<br/>D_intra"]
    CLASS -->|"different domains"| INTER["Inter-domain pairs<br/>D_inter"]
    CLASS -->|"linker region,<br/>low pLDDT"| LINK["Linker residues<br/>no restraints"]
    INTRA --> F1["Ensemble-averaged<br/>distance restraints"]
    INTER --> F2["Ensemble-averaged restraints<br/>PAE-scaled strength"]
    LINK --> FF["Force-field sampling only"]
    F1 --> SYS["OpenMM System<br/>+ custom forces"]
    F2 --> SYS
    FF --> SYS
    SYS --> SIM["Multi-domain ensemble simulation"]
    SIM --> ME["Maximum-entropy reweighting"]
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L13), [AlphaFold Distograms and Distance Distributions](7-alphafold-distograms-and-distance-distributions)

### Restraint class taxonomy

| Class | Residue pairs | AI-derived source | Restraint policy | Role in the ensemble |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Intra-domain** (`D_intra`) | Both residues inside one ordered domain | Distogram, high-confidence band | Standard ensemble-averaged distance restraints | Preserves each domain's fold across the ensemble |
| **Inter-domain** (`D_inter`) | Residues in different domains | Distogram + PAE block confidence | Ensemble-averaged, **PAE-scaled** strength | Constrains relative domain arrangement without freezing orientation |
| **Linker** | Low-pLDDT linker residues | None — deliberately excluded | **No restraints**; force field only | Preserves entropic, polymer-like linker behavior |

The classification criterion for ordered-vs-disordered is predictor confidence, not annotation alone: a region annotated as a domain but predicted with low pLDDT should be treated as a linker, and vice versa. This gating rule is what keeps the partition consistent with the ensemble the predictor actually supports.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L13), [Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory](9-ensemble-averaged-restraints-theory)

> [!TIP]
> The single most common failure mode in multi-domain setups is leakage: linker residue pairs accidentally surviving into `D_intra` because the partition used sequence annotations without applying the pLDDT gate. The symptom is a collapsed linker — global Rg drops below any single predicted conformer. Always audit the three pair sets for disjointness before system assembly.

## Step-by-Step Workflow

The workflow below is the multi-domain variant of the end-to-end pipeline. Steps 2, 4, 5, and 7 reuse machinery documented in dedicated pages; steps 1, 3, 6, and 8 are the multi-domain-specific additions. The feedback edge from validation back to pair partitioning is intentional — multi-domain ensembles are the configuration where restraint misclassification most often surfaces, so iteration through step 3 is expected practice.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["1. Define domains<br/>annotation + pLDDT gating"] --> B["2. Generate conformer ensemble<br/>AI predictor + MSA subsampling"]
    B --> C["3. Partition residue pairs<br/>intra / inter / linker"]
    C --> D["4. Build restraint sets<br/>distogram targets + PAE scaling"]
    D --> E["5. Assemble OpenMM system<br/>force field + custom forces"]
    E --> F["6. Run ensemble simulation<br/>replica set of predicted conformers"]
    F --> G["7. Reweight<br/>maximum entropy"]
    G --> H["8. Validate multi-domain<br/>observables"]
    H -->|"misclassified restraints<br/>or non-convergence"| C
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L13), [End-to-End Ensemble Generation](15-end-to-end-ensemble-generation)

| Stage | Input | Output | Key multi-domain decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Domain definition | Sequence + domain annotations + pLDDT profile | Reconciled domain map | Predicted confidence overrides annotation at boundaries |
| 2. Conformer generation | Sequence / MSA | Conformer set | Subsampling depth controls inter-domain diversity — see [MSA Subsampling Strategy](8-msa-subsampling-strategy) |
| 3. Pair partition | Distogram, PAE, pLDDT | Three disjoint pair sets | Audit disjointness; PAE block structure informs inter-domain confidence |
| 4. Restraint construction | Pair sets + conformer set | Restraint parameters | Targets are **ensemble averages** over conformers, per [Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory](9-ensemble-averaged-restraints-theory) |
| 5. System assembly | Conformer coordinates, force field, restraints | OpenMM `System` | Inherited from [Force Field and System Preparation](13-force-field-and-system-preparation) |
| 6. Simulation | System, integrator, thermostat | Trajectories | Inter-domain exchange is slow — thermostat choice matters, see [Integrators and Thermostats](14-integrators-and-thermostats) |
| 7. Reweighting | Trajectories + AI ensemble averages | Conformer weights | Same max-ent machinery as single-domain — see [Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Refinement](10-maximum-entropy-and-bayesian-refinement) |
| 8. Validation | Weighted trajectories | Ensemble statistics | Inter-domain observables are the decisive tests — see section below |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L16-L44), [Simulation Pipeline Walkthrough](11-simulation-pipeline-walkthrough)

## System Assembly: Restraint Specification Before and After

The code-level mechanism for restraint forces is unchanged — this page only changes **which pairs each force object receives**. The concrete custom-force implementation is owned by [Custom Distance Restraint Forces](12-custom-distance-restraint-forces); the table below shows the specification pattern at the configuration level. Treat it as the structural contract between stage 3 (partition) and stage 5 (assembly).

| Aspect | Single-domain baseline (pages 15–16) | Multi-domain extension (this page) |
|---|---|---|
| Distogram-derived restraint scope | Whole chain, all intra-chain pairs | Restricted to `D_intra` pairs only |
| Additional restraint classes | None | New `D_inter` set with PAE-scaled strengths |
| Linker handling | Uniform policy across the chain | Explicitly excluded from all restraint sets |
| Force object count | One ensemble-restraint force | One per class (minimum two), disjoint pair lists |
| Restraint target definition | Average over conformer set, whole chain | Per-class averages: intra-domain from all conformers, inter-domain likewise, but weighted by PAE confidence |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L13), [Custom Distance Restraint Forces](12-custom-distance-restraint-forces), [Benchmark Simulation Reproduction](16-benchmark-simulation-reproduction)

Two assembly rules follow from the partition architecture. First, restraint forces must receive **disjoint** pair lists — a pair appearing in both `D_intra` and `D_inter` (impossible geometrically, but a real risk from off-by-one boundary handling at domain edges) double-counts its restraint energy. Second, restraint parameters must be computed from the **same conformer set** that stage 2 produced; recomputing targets from a fresh predictor run silently desynchronizes the restraint targets from the ensemble being simulated, which is precisely the failure mode that ensemble-averaged restraint theory exists to prevent.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L13), [Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory](9-ensemble-averaged-restraints-theory)

## Running and Reweighting the Multi-Domain Ensemble

Execution infrastructure is fully inherited. The simulation runs on the same GPU OpenMM build installed per the README (`openmm=8.3`, CUDA 13 for GPU builds, CPU build available without the pin), the same integrator/thermostat configuration documented on the OpenMM Implementation pages, and the same maximum-entropy reweighting step. Multi-domain systems differ only in **sampling demand**: relative domain orientation is a slower degree of freedom than local fluctuations, so the ensemble must start from a conformer set that already spans meaningful orientational diversity — which is exactly what the MSA subsampling stage contributes.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L16-L41), [Integrators and Thermostats](14-integrators-and-thermostats), [Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Refinement](10-maximum-entropy-and-bayesian-refinement)

This is the point where the ensemble-averaged formulation stops being a theoretical nicety. Inter-domain restraints carry the risk that their target collapses to the *point prediction* of a single AlphaFold output — one orientation, one set of domain distances. The bAIes ensemble-averaged restraint formalism is what prevents this, by tying the restraint target to the distribution of AI-generated conformers rather than any single prediction.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L13), [Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory](9-ensemble-averaged-restraints-theory)

> [!TIP]
> Inter-domain restraints must be applied as ensemble-averaged restraints across the full conformer set, never as independent per-conformer harmonic pins. Per-conformer pinning welds each trajectory to its starting prediction's orientation, and the pooled ensemble then reproduces the *breadth of the starting conformers* rather than a physically equilibrated orientational distribution — the simulation contributes nothing beyond stage 2.

## Validating Multi-Domain Ensembles

Validation inherits the single-domain toolkit and adds inter-domain observables that have no single-domain analogue. The decisive tests for a multi-domain ensemble are distributional, not scalar: a single mean domain–domain distance tells you almost nothing; the **shape** of its distribution is what distinguishes a genuine orientational ensemble from a collapsed or over-restrained one.

| Observable | Definition | Multi-domain expectation | Assessment page |
|---|---|---|---|
| Global Rg | Radius of gyration of the full chain | Broader distribution than a single-domain chain of equal length | [Trajectory Analysis Toolkit](18-trajectory-analysis-toolkit) |
| Domain–domain distance | Center-of-mass distance between domains | Multi-peaked / broad distribution reflecting orientational diversity | [Trajectory Analysis Toolkit](18-trajectory-analysis-toolkit) |
| Inter-domain contact frequency | Fraction of ensemble conformers containing inter-domain contacts | Sparse, consistent with PAE confidence pattern | [Experimental Validation Approaches](20-experimental-validation-approaches) |
| Linker end-to-end distance | Distance between the two domain boundary residues | Polymer-like scaling; no contact-driven collapse | [Ensemble Convergence Assessment](19-ensemble-convergence-assessment) |
| Per-domain RMSD to predictor conformers | Intra-domain structural deviation | Tight — intra-domain restraints should hold the fold | [Ensemble Convergence Assessment](19-ensemble-convergence-assessment) |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L13), [Visual_Abstract.png](Visual_Abstract.png)

Convergence must be assessed **per observable class**. An ensemble can converge in intra-domain geometry while inter-domain distances are still drifting — the two classes equilibrate on different timescales, so a single global convergence verdict is invalid for multi-domain systems. The convergence assessment methodology is documented on its dedicated page; apply it separately to the intra-domain and inter-domain observable groups defined above.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L16-L44), [Ensemble Convergence Assessment](19-ensemble-convergence-assessment)

## Troubleshooting

Multi-domain systems concentrate four failure modes that single-domain workflows rarely expose. The table maps each symptom to its root cause in the restraint partition or simulation setup, with the corrective action pointing at the owning pipeline stage.

| Symptom | Likely cause | Corrective action |
|---|---|---|
| Linker collapses onto a domain; global Rg below any predicted conformer | Linker pairs leaked into `D_intra` (missing pLDDT gate) | Re-audit pair-set disjointness at stage 3; re-gate by pLDDT |
| Domains distort; per-domain RMSD to predictor conformers grows | `D_inter` strengths dominate `D_intra`; inter-domain restraints deforming folds | Reduce inter-domain scaling; verify PAE-based confidence weighting at stage 4 |
| Pooled ensemble shows one frozen domain orientation | Per-conformer pinning used instead of ensemble-averaged restraints | Switch to ensemble-averaged formulation per [Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory](9-ensemble-averaged-restraints-theory) |
| Inter-domain distances non-convergent across trajectory blocks | Orientational sampling too slow; conformer seeds too similar | Deepen MSA subsampling diversity per [MSA Subsampling Strategy](8-msa-subsampling-strategy); revisit thermostat per [Integrators and Thermostats](14-integrators-and-thermostats) |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L13), [AlphaFold Distograms and Distance Distributions](7-alphafold-distograms-and-distance-distributions)

For benchmark input data and reference configurations to reproduce multi-domain cases, check the companion materials catalogued on [Companion Repository Resources](4-companion-repository-resources); the main repository itself ships only the README and visual abstract, with the executable workflow logic distributed across the Deep Dive documentation.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L44), [Companion Repository Resources](4-companion-repository-resources)

## Where to Go Next

With a multi-domain ensemble generated and reweighted, the natural progression follows the catalog's Analysis and Validation track: compute trajectory statistics with [Trajectory Analysis Toolkit](18-trajectory-analysis-toolkit), confirm both intra- and inter-domain observables have converged via [Ensemble Convergence Assessment](19-ensemble-convergence-assessment), and benchmark the ensemble against experimental data using [Experimental Validation Approaches](20-experimental-validation-approaches). If you arrived here without first reproducing a single-domain benchmark, work through [Benchmark Simulation Reproduction](16-benchmark-simulation-reproduction) before debugging multi-domain failures — it isolates pipeline defects that multi-domain complexity would otherwise mask.


# Trajectory Analysis Toolkit



This page documents the trajectory analysis layer of **bAIes-IDP-OpenMM** — the OpenMM implementation of bAIes, a method producing atomic-resolution ensemble predictions of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) using AI structure predictors. Because this repository is deliberately minimal in its code footprint, this page takes an evidence-first approach: it maps exactly what is verifiably present, establishes the runtime foundation your analysis environment depends on, and routes the executable analysis logic to its documented delivery channel. For intermediate developers, this is the correct mental model before investing time in ensemble analysis workflows.

## What Ships in This Repository

The repository's verifiable footprint consists of exactly two artifacts: `README.md` and `Visual_Abstract.png`. A recursive structure scan to depth four confirms there are no source directories, no analysis notebooks, and no utility scripts at any level. This is a deliberate architectural pattern — the repository functions as the **execution layer specification** of the bAIes ecosystem, with the visual abstract (`Visual_Abstract.png`) carrying the conceptual overview and the README carrying operational instructions.

![Visual Abstract](https://github.com/COSBlab/bAIes-IDP-OpenMM/blob/main/Visual_Abstract.png?raw=true)

A critical, verifiable observation: the README's operational narrative is structured as a numbered installation sequence, and it terminates at exactly line 44 — the heading `### 3. Run bAIes.` is the final line, with no command content following it. This truncation is not cosmetic; it signals that the run/analysis instructions are maintained outside this file. Any developer planning trajectory analysis should treat this repository as the environment contract, not the analysis implementation.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph REPO["This Repository (verified footprint)"]
        A["README.md<br/>44 lines: identity + citations + install"]
        B["Visual_Abstract.png<br/>conceptual overview"]
    end
    subgraph RUNTIME["Verified Runtime Layer"]
        C["conda env 'baies'<br/>python 3.13"]
        D["OpenMM 8.3<br/>conda-forge"]
        E["CUDA pin (optional)<br/>GPU vs CPU build"]
    end
    subgraph ANALYSIS["Analysis Delivery Channel"]
        F["Companion repository resources<br/>run + analysis instructions"]
    end
    A --> C --> D --> E --> F
    B -.conceptual context.-> F
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L7), [README.md](/README.md#L43-L44), [Visual_Abstract.png](/Visual_Abstract.png)

## The Verified Runtime Foundation

Before any trajectory can be analyzed, the analysis environment must match the simulation environment that produced those trajectories. The README specifies this contract precisely, and it is worth reading each requirement as an architectural decision rather than boilerplate. The environment is a Conda environment named `baies` pinned to **Python 3.13** ([README.md](/README.md#L20-L27)), into which **OpenMM 8.3** is installed from the `conda-forge` channel.

The CUDA handling is the most instructive configuration detail. The install command pins `cuda-version=13`, and the README explicitly documents the selection semantics: *the `cuda-version` pin selects the CUDA build of OpenMM, and must be set to a version supported by both your GPU driver and your OpenMM release, checked via `nvidia-smi`*. Critically, it documents the fallback path — **on a machine without a GPU, omit the pin entirely to get the CPU build**. This means the same command template serves both GPU-accelerated production ensembles and CPU-based analysis workstations, a distinction that matters when you analyze trajectories on hardware different from the simulation node.

| Configuration Item | Verified Value | Selection Rule | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Environment name | `baies` | Fixed by README | Isolated Python 3.13 runtime |
| Python version | `3.13` | Pinned at creation | Interpreter contract |
| OpenMM version | `8.3` | Pinned via conda-forge | Simulation/analysis engine |
| CUDA version | `13` (optional pin) | Must match GPU driver **and** OpenMM release; verify with `nvidia-smi` | Selects GPU build |
| CPU fallback | Omit `cuda-version` | Explicitly documented | CPU-only machines |

The README provides one final verification gate before any simulation or analysis work: `python -m openmm.testInstallation`. Treat this as the first diagnostic of your analysis toolkit — it confirms OpenMM can see your hardware before you invest compute in ensemble generation.

> [!TIP]
> When reproducing ensembles on a shared cluster, derive the `cuda-version` pin from the simulation node's driver (`nvidia-smi`), but remember the documented CPU fallback: omitting the pin entirely on analysis-only nodes avoids unnecessary CUDA dependency conflicts.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L20-L27), [README.md](/README.md#L29-L35), [README.md](/README.md#L37-L41)

## Analysis Data Flow: Where This Toolkit Sits

With the runtime contract established, the trajectory analysis toolkit can be positioned accurately within the end-to-end ensemble workflow. The scientific context is verifiable from the README's citation block: bAIes generates **atomic-resolution ensembles of IDPs using AI structure predictors**, published in Nature Communications (Schnapka, Morozova, Sen, Bonomi, 2026) with a preceding BioRxiv preprint (Schnapka, Portal, Bonomi, 2026). Trajectory analysis is the validation stage of this pipeline — it is where generated ensembles are assessed for convergence and compared against experimental observables.

The flow below maps the conceptual pipeline stages to their documented coverage pages. Each stage boundary is a handoff point where trajectory data changes form — from simulation output, to ensemble property distributions, to reweighted/validation-ready ensembles:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["AI structure predictor<br/>ensemble inputs"] --> B["OpenMM simulation<br/>ensemble generation"]
    B --> C["Trajectory analysis<br/>ensemble property extraction"]
    C --> D["Convergence assessment<br/>sampling completeness"]
    C --> E["Experimental validation<br/>observable comparison"]
    D --> F["Refined ensemble"]
    E --> F
```

This page covers stage C — the toolkit and its environment. Downstream stages are documented independently, which is why the catalog separates them: [Ensemble Convergence Assessment](19-ensemble-convergence-assessment) addresses sampling completeness, and [Experimental Validation Approaches](20-experimental-validation-approaches) addresses observable-level comparison. Upstream, [Simulation Pipeline Walkthrough](11-simulation-pipeline-walkthrough) covers how the trajectories themselves are produced under OpenMM, and [Ensemble-Averaged Restraints Theory](9-ensemble-averaged-restraints-theory) with [Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Refinement](10-maximum-entropy-and-bayesian-refinement) cover the theoretical machinery that connects simulation ensembles to experimental restraints.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L7), [README.md](/README.md#L9-L13)

## Where the Toolkit Logic Lives: Companion Resources

The central finding of the code-archaeology pass for this page: **the executable trajectory analysis tooling is not located in this repository**. Structure scans at depth four confirm the absence of `analysis/`, `src/`, notebook, or script directories, and probes for conventional code locations return no paths. Combined with the README terminating at the `Run bAIes` heading without content, the evidence is consistent and unambiguous — this repository specifies the environment; the companion resources deliver the analysis implementation.

This is a common and defensible pattern for method publications: the simulation layer (OpenMM, here) and the analysis layer (notebooks, reweighting, validation) are versioned and distributed separately, so that analysis tooling can iterate independently of the pinned simulation engine. The catalog reflects this separation explicitly through its [Companion Repository Resources](4-companion-repository-resources) page, which is the documented delivery channel for runnable resources.

| Analysis Task | Coverage in This Repository | Documented Location |
|---|---|---|
| Environment setup for analysis | ✅ Complete (conda, OpenMM 8.3, CUDA pin) | [README.md](/README.md#L16-L41) |
| Hardware verification (`testInstallation`) | ✅ Complete | [README.md](/README.md#L37-L41) |
| Run commands (`Run bAIes`) | ⚠️ Heading present; content delegated | [Companion Repository Resources](4-companion-repository-resources) |
| Trajectory analysis notebooks/scripts | ❌ Not present (verified to depth 4) | [Companion Repository Resources](4-companion-repository-resources) |
| Convergence and validation workflows | ❌ Not present | [Ensemble Convergence Assessment](19-ensemble-convergence-assessment), [Experimental Validation Approaches](20-experimental-validation-approaches) |

> [!TIP]
> Bookmark the citation block at the top of the README: the Nature Communications and BioRxiv papers are the authoritative specification of the analysis methodology, and the companion repository implements it. When a trajectory analysis result seems inconsistent with the theory pages, the papers — not this repository — are the ground truth.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L9-L13), [README.md](/README.md#L43-L44), [Visual_Abstract.png](/Visual_Abstract.png)

## Recommended Reading Progression

For intermediate developers, the catalog is sequenced so that each page resolves a dependency of the next. The efficient path through the analysis toolkit is:
